en: Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Kālī has innumerable enemies; Pañcamī is likewise innumerable; Tripurā is innumerable, as is Bālā; Hṛdilocanā is innumerable. (1) I shall describe the Vīracūḍāmaṇi, the Mahānīla, according to the proper sequence;

by this sequential yoga, it bestows very swift results. (2) The practitioner, having risen at dawn, should remember his Guru with reverence; having meditated upon the Great Heroic Guru, or else upon the lineage of the Ṛṣis and Gurus, (3) he should worship Vīrabhadra in due order with the five offerings.

I salute the Hero, the treasury of compassion, who wears blue garments, is adorned with blue unguents, whose body is decorated with conch shells and other ornaments, who is joyful, possesses two eyes, and has his blue Śakti seated upon the lap of his left side. (4) Having meditated upon the supreme deity, Nīlasundarī, within the heart—one who is short-statured, blue, large-eyed, adorned with the five mudrās, (5) holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga in her hands, bearing a sword and a blue lotus, with a mass of matted hair entwined with a garland of serpents, and possessing full, elevated breasts—[one should worship].

(6) Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who is endowed with fresh youth and whose eyes roll with intoxication, the practitioner shall become omniscient. (7) The wise one should perform the visualization of the Vidyā through the union of the Hero and the Haṃsa; out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall explain the Haṃsa-sādhana. (8) By the mere knowledge of which one becomes omniscient and conquers the earth; the Blessed One, whose essence is the Haṃsa, always recites the Jīva-mantra. (9) [The fruit] of its recollection...

By this alone, a man becomes liberated while living; he is declared to be a *ṛṣi*, a *haṃsa*, and always a *paramahaṃsa*. (10) For the sake of attaining yoga, there is the application (*viniyoga*) of the unmanifest *gāyatrī* chant. To the Sun-self, O Goddess, one should assign the heart; likewise, to the Moon-self, the head. (11) The stainless light is the tuft (*śikhā*), and those who are beyond appearance are the others. One should place the feet of the Infinite One upon the eyes of the Unmanifest. (12) Having thus performed the monthly rite, beginning with Gaṇeśa and the others...

One should offer six hundred oblations to Gaṇeśa, six thousand to Prajāpati, six thousand to Gadāpāṇi (the mace-bearer), six thousand to Pinākin (the wielder of the trident), one thousand to the Ātman, and one thousand to the Paramātman. One thousand are for the Guru; this is the ritual procedure according to the injunctions. One should offer six hundred oblations to the red-colored Gaṇeśa at the Mūlādhāra, which has four petals and is joined with the letters beginning with *va* and ending with *la*. [Then] the Svādhiṣṭhāna...

One should offer the six musical instruments, such as the drum and the *ābhāṅkhaṭ*, together with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, to Brahmā. On each petal, which possesses the brilliance of a mass of lightning, one should recite ten syllables for each; saluting Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, one should present six thousand [verses]. On the twelve petals, which have the luster of a great sapphire, one should salute Umā and Maheśvara and offer six thousand [verses]. On the pure, smoke-colored [petals], the *kalāpa*...

One should place the three lords [in the three eyes], and offer a thousand salutations to the Self as the power of vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*). In the *ājñā* [cakra], which has the luster of lightning, one should contemplate two white teeth. One should offer a thousand [salutations] to the Supreme Self, the Supreme Power.

O Goddess, in this ocean-like [body] with mountains for breasts and islands for the navel, I bow to you, O Consort of Viṣṇu; forgive the touch of my feet. O Goddess, one should place the foot according to the comfort of the self. Or [one may do so]...

One should perform the impurity-rites and the like, and practice the bath of ashes. Seated in the *vīrāsana* posture and smeared with heroic ashes (23), the wise one, having meditated upon the Hero, O Great Goddess, should worship the Heroic Garland and offer it one thousand and eight times into his left hand (24). O lady of excellent hips, he should use sacrificial flowers for cleaning the teeth; O Maheśānī, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and touch his own limbs with the Śakti. He should then manifest the gestures of love, such as the *hāva* and *bhāva*.

One should perform the rites for oneself according to the Mahāvīra-krama and satisfy Nīlasarasvatī. O Goddess, one should satisfy the Trimūrti, who is exceedingly white due to leprosy (*arśas*). Having uttered the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), one should then say "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi namaḥ*). Thereafter, one should satisfy Tārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlā. Then, O Goddess, having performed the three *ācamanas* and the three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should take [the water] with the left hand and consecrate it three times. Having sprinkled it thrice upon the head, one should discharge the *vajra* weapon of water. O Maheśānī, one should utter Viyat (H), Vahni (R), and Nārāyaṇa (Ū) with the *bindu*; then utter Māyā (Hrīṃ) along with Sakala; then Gaganam (Ha) joined with Vahni (Ra), equal to the half-moon.

One should utter the syllable *Ha* adorned with the left eye (*I*), followed by the solar orb (*Ra*) and the letter *Ga*. Having recited the word *Tārā*, one should join the palms in *añjali* at the heart. The wise practitioner should then chant the *Gāyatrī* mantra eight or twelve times. Having uttered the *Vāgbhava* (*Aiṃ*), one says: "We know the One with the Single Braid" (*ekajaṭāyai vidmahe*). Then, having uttered *Trīṃ*, one says: "To the Blue Sarasvatī, we meditate" (*nīlasarasvatyai dhīmahi*). Having uttered the *Hṛllekhā* (*Hrīṃ*), one says: "May she impel us toward Tārā" (*tannaḥ tāre pracodayāt*). After chanting, one should perform the offering of the merit into the left hand of the deity. [Thus ends the first chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. Now I shall describe the Great Blue Rite (*Mahānīlakrama*) for the benefit of practitioners.

Through mere knowledge of the *māyāyāga*, the practitioner becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*). The supreme practitioner should accomplish [this] through the division of the *āmnāya-cakras*: the Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern, and that which is beyond the North.

These are, in sequence: the Śākta, the Śaiva, the Guru, the Saura, and the Vaiṣṇava. In the Eastern *āmnāya* is the Great Goddess, the venerable Tripurasundarī. Likewise, the Gāṇapatya, Saura, and Vaiṣṇava [traditions] follow in the Southern sequence.

O lotus-eyed one, the Raudra, Bhairava, and Śaiva [traditions] belong to the West. The divisions of the Northern *āmnāya* are Ugrarā, Ugrārtitāriṇī, and others. In the Upper *āmnāya* is the Great Vidyā of the Śāmbhava tradition.

O auspicious one, seated upon five corpses and bestowing protection, one should worship the five-faced Maheśvara Aghora and Kākinī thereafter. One should worship the goddess Caitanyabhairavī and Sadyojāta in the west; and in the north, one should worship the one named Bhairava Kuvera and Maheśvara Vāmadeva. Afterwards, the supreme practitioner should worship Ghorabhairavī in the northeast according to the specific sequence of the tradition (āmnāya). By means of the method of the Gandharva lineage, one should worship the five Bhairavīs. Tripurā, the Supreme Goddess, should mount the seat of the five corpses. Śu...

One should mount a dark-blue horse made of perfected crystal, O Tara, the savior of the world of beings. Therein lie the secret signs of the Krama, the secret signs of ritual action (*kriyā*), the secret signs of the yantra, and likewise the secret signs of the worship of the deity;

the secret signs of the flower, the secret signs of the Shakti, and the secret signs of the Guru according to the specific *kulācāra*. O Goddess, without these secret signs, an obstruction to spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises.

O Varārohā, one who always delights in the dark blue [practice] should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) with devotion; otherwise, an obstruction to the accomplishment of the mantras of other deities arises. One should gaze upon the world with power.

O Kaṃsāri, one should worship the yantra marked with *vajrapuṣpa* flowers using *vajrapuṣpa*. Abandoning all wretchedness of action, the best of practitioners should accomplish his goal. O Goddess, one should worship the root-yantra according to the secret conventions of the yantra; at the time of worship, one should especially not utter the names of Hari. Abandoning other perfumes, one should use sandalwood and red sandalwood; having worshipped with red flowers, one should avoid *bilva* leaves. One should diligently avoid *tulasī*, *malinī*, and *dhātrī*. O Lord of Gods, even without a consort, one may perform recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), meditation, worship, and so forth.

Obstruction to all success arises; one should abandon substances such as ground flour and flowers, and specifically avoid food products. One should worship ten substances, especially those produced from grain. One should always dwell alone in a forest, on a mountain, at a crossroads, or in a cremation ground—this is the characteristic of a hero (*vīra*). A hero is courageous, compassionate, free from anger, and has conquered his senses; he is constantly devoted to righteous action—this is the characteristic of a hero. Non-violent, a knower of the scriptures, devoid of greed and anger, and having abandoned delusion and deceit—one is indeed called a hero (*vīru*). [He should serve] the lineage of gurus...

The worship of the Goddess is not in vain; one should worship the Guru of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), and one should worship Akṣobhya. One should worship the three Nāgas according to the lineage of the Goddess’s oral transmission. O Maheśānī, the worship of the Vīras occurs when the watch of the night has passed. Having established [the deities] according to the rite, one should perform worship and offer libations in the vessels of the Vīras. One should not observe a fast, nor should one practice any other austerity. One should not eat the *pāṭara* fish; if it is not obtained, one should simply abstain from eating it. One should not eat food prepared with oil; one should avoid such things in sacrifices. One should not sit on a very high seat, nor sleep in a bed within the darkness. One should not revile the circle of Yoginīs, nor should one revile the [Gurus].

One-eyed, constantly devoted to service for the guru, and intent on the worship of heroes; one who renounces the wealth of others and abandons the wives of others; one who renounces speaking ill of others, censuring them, and harboring hatred toward others; and one who renounces desire for the property of the guru and desire for the power of a hero—these become Brahma-rākṣasas dwelling in the Raurava hell. Without initiation there is no worship, and without worship there is no sexual union; without initiation there is no meat [offering]—one would go to the Raurava hell. One should not worship the Śakti during the day, nor look upon her when she is naked; one should worship her at night, especially in a triangular mandala.

One should not accumulate wealth, O Great Mistress; nor should one ever, without hesitation, cause a breach in the circle of the tradition (*āmnāya-cakra*). Constantly devoted to meditation on the Guru and intent upon his worship, one should especially worship the Guru’s wife and his *śakti*. [Thus ends the second chapter in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*. Now I shall explain initiation (*dīkṣā*) out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, by the mere knowledge of which an adept becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*).

One who is pure-minded, compassionate, a Brahmin well-versed in the Vedas, constantly devoted to the Kula conduct, an expounder of the Kula scriptures, peaceful, and self-controlled—[such a person is fit].

Free from all passion, greed, and delusion, having abandoned anger and hypocrisy, and being intent on the worship of women—one endowed with such characteristics should worship the Guru with reverence. The disciple, who has mastered the mantras, is devoted to the Guru, avoids the wives of others, refrains from harming others, and abstains from the wealth of others; who is a giver and an enjoyer, yet specifically free from latent desires and worldly indulgence; who is constantly engaged in the rites of Brahman and devoted to the worship of Śakti—a disciple endowed with these characteristics possesses his own authority. In the Mahācīna-krama, there is no fault regarding Nīlaśāradā, nor in the worship of Siddhā, Aruṇā, or Tārā.

For men, there is no requirement for purifying the zodiacal signs (*rāśi-cakra*), nor for the wheel of wealth (*dhana-cakra*), nor for restrictions regarding months, fortnights, lunar days (*tithi*), or constellations (*nakṣatra*); nor are Tuesdays and Saturdays to be avoided as days. Having constructed the mandala according to the rules, one should provide banners, a canopy, and archways adorned with serpents. O Great Lord, one should fashion the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as a triangle, a half-moon, a vulva-shaped pit (*yonikuṇḍa*), or likewise a curved, circular, square, octagonal, or hexagonal shape. It should be joined with a girdle (*mekhalā*) and a vulva, and be characterized by a neck and a navel. O Great Lord, prior to initiation, the ritual sowing of seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should be performed on an auspicious day at a favorable moment during the morning.

Having invoked the Guru and the deities, one should perform the washing of their feet, saluting them again and again. One should worship the Brahmins with *madhuparka* and cause them to recite the *svasti* benediction.

With the mantras "Devasya tvā," "Sūrāstvā," and likewise the *Pāvamāna* hymns, as well as the *Lakṣmī-sūkta*, the *Devī-sūkta*, the *Rudra-sūkta*, and especially the *Rakṣoghna* hymns, one should consecrate the Brahmins and cause them to recite the *svasti*.

Without the worship of Kālikā, there should be prostration, rising up, and then the *añjali* gesture. Having drawn the *Vāstu-maṇḍala*, one should worship the *Bali-pūraka*. This is the procedure for the worship of the Nine Planets (*Navagraha*) and the Great Rudra (*Mahārudra*) sacrifice.

Then, when the second day has arrived, having performed the morning rites, one should next perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), as well as the installation (pratiṣṭhā) and the vitalization (prāṇa). One should perform the three-fold Mātṛkā-nyāsa—creation, dissolution, and maintenance—and especially the nyāsa prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa), O Maheśānī. The twice-born [priest] should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth, and recite the Śāntipāṭha. Having specifically proclaimed the place and time, and having declared, "I shall perform the commencement and the initiation (dīkṣā) of the mantra," first [one should perform] the eighteen purifications of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) individually, beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa) by the root mantra.

Sprinkling is performed with the mantra and the arrow; likewise, striking is done with that same [mantra], while sprinkling with *darbha* grass is prescribed with the *varma* (armor) mantra. O Goddess, digging is done with the *astra* (weapon) mantra, filling with the *hṛd* (heart) mantra, leveling with the *astra*, and likewise sprinkling with the *varma*. Compacting is done with the *hūṃ* mantra, while cleansing is done with the *varma* itself. With that same [mantra], one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and contemplate the form of the *kuṅkala*. Afterwards, one should worship the transformation into a trident with the *namaḥ* mantra.

The transformation into a thunderbolt (*vajrīkaraṇa*) is done with the *astra* mantra, and one should recite the *namaḥ* mantra. O Goddess, the spreading with *kuśa* grass is done with the *kavaca* (armor), but the lines should be drawn with the *hṛd* mantra, as it has been declared.

Beginning from the western direction of the Varuṇa-line and proceeding toward the east, one should worship Viṣṇu, Viśveśa, and Śakra in sequence on the eastern-pointed lines. One should also worship Virañci, Yama, and Candra on the north-pointed lines. Thereupon, one should draw a beautiful triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and an eight-petaled lotus. One should perform the sprinkling with the *Tāra* (Om) mantra and worship the Yoga-pīṭha.

One should worship Vāgīśvarī—who resembles a blue lotus and has bathed after her menses—united with Vāgīśvara, using the ritual offerings (*upacāras*). A Kula woman or one made of clay may serve as the preceptor (*ācārya*).

The preceptor should cause [the fire] to be offered; having touched the fire, he should abandon the portion for the *kravyāda* (flesh-eating spirits). Having discarded a single ember in the south-western direction (*naiṛtyā*), the teacher should perform the fourfold supreme consecration (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*). He should contemplate the mantra of the three fires as far as the *audarya* and *divya* [consecrations]. Having conjoined it with the fire-mantra and the *tāra* (Oṃ), he should consecrate it. Having rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, he should then protect it with the *astra-mantra*. Having veiled it with the *tantra-mantra*, he should worship it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Having uttered the *tāra*, O Goddess of Gods, he should circumambulate the fire three times. [He should then utter] the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*).

One should place [the offering] into the womb of the Noble Goddess; thereafter, O Lord of Gods, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and so forth during sexual union. Having worshipped with all the ritual services (*upacāra*), one should then kindle the fire. Reciting "O Citpiṅgala," then "Hanu-yugma," then "Daha," again "Paca-yugma," O Maheśānī, and "Sarvajña ājñāpaya," one should utter the wife of Fire (the *svāhā* mantra) and, having kindled it, begin the meditation: "I revere the blazing fire, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations, golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and facing in all directions. O Maheśānī, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own body and place the tongue [mantra]. Hiraṇyā-ga...

O Maheśānī, one should extract the syllable *svā* which is exceedingly red, joined with fire (*ra*), and the seed-syllable of wind (*ya*) endowed with the left ear (*u*), adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*.

One should place each one individually on the deity’s limbs: on the feet, the two shanks, the head, the face, the nose, and the eyes; thereafter, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) and carry out the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*). O Goddess, [the mantras are]: *sahasrārciṣe* for the heart; *svasti pūrṇam* for the head; *uttiṣṭha puruṣa* for the crown of the head (*śīrṣa*); *dhūmravyāpinī saptajihvāya* for the armor (*kavaca*).

One should place the Eye and the Wielder of the Bow (Astra) [in the two eyes]. O Maheśānī, the wise one should perform the Nyāsa of the Eight Forms (Aṣṭamūrti). O Maheśānī, one should place [the mantra] "To Agni Jātavedas" on the head; "To Saptajihva" on the right shoulder; and "To Havyavāhana" on the left. O Maheśānī, one should place "To Aṣṭodara" on the right foot and "To Vaiśvānara" on the left. Having placed "To Kumāratejas" on the waist, one should place "Viśvamukha"—the face of all the gods—on the left hip. Having honored the Fire with the mantra "Prasava," one should afterwards prepare the seat. One should sprinkle it with water mixed with Kuśa grass and spread the ritual coverings around it.

One should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) behind [the fire], avoiding the direction of the cow-slayer (the southwest). One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva in the order of the enclosing sticks. Having meditated upon the deity consisting of fire, O Goddess, one should honor him with perfumes and other offerings.

Reciting the mantra of Agni, one should perform the worship and the *homa*. The mantra for accomplishing the fire is as follows: "O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come hither! O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites! After this, one should utter the wife of the fire (*vahnijāyā*). Thereafter, one should worship Hiraṇyā and the others in the hexagon in their proper order. Then one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*), especially on the filaments (*kesara*).

Having worshipped the eight-formed Lord well, one should worship [the deities] upon the eight petals; having honored the guardians of the directions (Dikpālas), one should sacrifice to them in order starting from the East. Taking the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and heating them while facing downward, one should purify the tip, middle, and base separately with a blade of *darbha* grass. Then, taking the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), one should sprinkle it with water using the Astra-mantra. Having poured the clarified butter into it, one should gaze upon it with the four rites beginning with *vīkṣaṇa*. Then, having cast a single ember toward the Vāyu direction according to the rules, and having carefully placed the *ājyasthālī* there, one should perform the heating. Having cast a pair of blazing *darbha* blades into the clarified butter, one should look at it in the fire.

Furthermore, the purification with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra) is prescribed; having ignited two blades of darbha grass, one should cast them invisibly into the fire. One who is accomplishing the removal of the cooking vessel (sthālī-udvāsana) should perform the illumination (udyotana). He should touch water and cast the embers into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); he should cast them out with the thumb and little finger while reciting the weapon-mantra (astramantra). This is indeed the purification (utpavana), the supreme procedure for consecration (saṃskāra). One should utter the "namas" mantra.

One should cast two *kuśa* blades face-to-face; thus one should perform the six purificatory rites (*ṣaṭ-saṃskāra*), including the sprinkling (*saṃplavana*). One should insert a pair of *kuśa* blades, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length, into the midst of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*). One should likewise contemplate the two parts as the white and black wings. One should contemplate the *iḍā* on the left side and the *piṅgalā* on the right, and having conceived the *suṣumṇā* in the middle, the excellent practitioner should perform the oblation (*homa*). To the three eyes—one on the right, one on the left, and one in the middle—one should offer oblations to Agni, Soma, and Agni-Soma. O Great Goddess, one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation into the mouth of the Fire.

Having contemplated the unity of that [deity], one should offer the *vyāhṛtis* beginning with the Vedas. With eight oblations offered by means of the *praṇava* while maintaining the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as *garbhādhāna*, the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should worship the fire and subsequently unite it with his own self.

He should offer oblations with five pieces of fuel-wood (*samidh*) soaked in clarified butter from the base to the tip. Then, he should offer each of the six limbs and the form-mantra (*mūrti-mantra*) with a single oblation. Having taken four portions of clarified butter and having joined the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles together, standing before the fire, he should then offer an oblation at the tip of the flame with the *śikhā* mantra. Having divided the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*) and the Lord of the Gaṇas (*gaṇādhipa*) into ten parts, he should contemplate the interior of the fire’s flames and offer ten oblations.

Then one should perform the joining of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna); thereafter, O Goddess, one should offer oblations for the principal limbs and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇa), one oblation for each. One should offer the Vyāhṛtis, O Goddess, and thereafter the "Brahmārpaṇa" [mantra]. Then one should again perform worship with the mantras along with the enclosures. One should offer three handfuls of flowers and place [the deity] upon the pedestal (pīṭha). Having drawn the support (ādhāra), one should draw a circular line and eight petals.

One should subsequently draw [the diagram] together with the pericarp and filaments, possessing four doors, adorned with vajras, and enchanting; thus equipped is this Yantra consisting of Śrī Tāriṇī. The Guru, facing east, while the other person faces north, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), should contemplate the universe as void. Having contemplated the Self as stainless, pure, and free from taint, consisting of Tāriṇī, he should contemplate the Goddess Tarpaṇā within the four-petaled Mūlādhāra, as a garland of shimmering syllables upon a blue lotus in a triangle. Having contemplated the mantra during the pouring [of the offering], he should complete the duration of time (kālā-mātrā). In the heart, upon the petals of the sun, [he should contemplate] the red [syllables].

One should contemplate a lotus; one should burn the female seed-syllable (*strīvīja*) and the universe, which is considered to consist of sixty-four forests. O Goddess, in that void, one should contemplate the void-natured seed-syllable of Māyā. Having contemplated the knife (*kartṛkā*) within this mantra, one should duly recollect, O Goddess, the showering stream of nectar according to the measure of thirty-two *mātrās*. In this manner, one should recollect one's own body as inherently pure and composed of Tāriṇī, situated in the midst of the orb of nectar—the power (*śakti*) known as Kalinī. Within the resonance (*nāda*), there is the wind; within that is the sound (*dhvani*); within that is the mantra; within the mantra is the light (*jyotis*); and at the end of that is the garlanded with points (*bindumālinī*). O Goddess, by contemplating in this way, one shall become a master of self-perfected powers (*siddhi*).

One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) and establish the vital breaths therein. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are proclaimed as its seers (*ṛṣis*). It is declared to be in the *chanda* of the *Gāyatrī*, with the deity known as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), who is the goddess consisting of all powers (*sarvaśaktimayī*); the application (*niyoga*) grants the perfection of the vital breaths. Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and place the *prāṇamantra* upon the heart. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows, O Great Lord: *āṃ* in the middle of the *ka*-group; *i īṃ* in the middle of the *ca*-group; *u ūṃ* in the middle of the *ṭa*-group; *e aiṃ* in the middle of the *ta*-group; *o auṃ* in the middle of the *pa*-group; and *śeṣaṃ* (the remainder) in the middle of the *ya*-group. Thus one should perform the placement.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs beginning with the heart: "Oṃ *hṛdayāya namaḥ*" for the heart; "Svāhā" at the end of "Oṃ *śirase*" for the head; "Vaṣaṭ" at the end for the placement of the crest-lock (*śikhā*); again "Hūṃ" at the end of "Oṃ *varmaṇe*" for the armor (*kavaca*); "Vauṣaṭ" at the end for the three eyes; and "Phaṭ" for the weapon (*astra*) on both hands. Having thus performed the procedure of placement, one should then perform the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*). Nārāyaṇa is said to be in the navel; Māyā (the syllable *Hrīṃ*) is in the middle of the north; the syllable *Aṃ* is above the soft Kuśa grass; the letter *Tva* is in the heart; blood (*asṛk*) is in the right shoulder; phlegm (*kapha*) is in the middle of the left shoulder; having placed fat (*medas*) in the left shoulder, one should place marrow (*majjā*) and bones (*asthi*) in the hands.

One should place the seed-syllable *Śukra* (Hrīm) on the right foot, or rather, one should deposit the *Vīrya* at the gateway. O Great Goddess, one should deposit [the mantra] from the head down to the feet with the *Krodha* [syllable]. One should extract the *Virajā* conjoined with the Moon (*Viṃdu*) and the *Lajjā-bīja*. Having uttered "Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ," one should say the words "my vital breaths" (*mamaprāṇa*). Then one should say: "my life-force, my vital breaths, mind, and all the senses; my speech, mind, skin, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths, come here! Stay happily for a long time! This mantra ends with the wife of Fire (*Svāhā*). O Goddess, one should extract the *Tāra* (Oṃ) and place it in the heart.

One should touch [the body] with the *stenasaṃsparśa* mantra and worship the *prāṇa-śakti* through the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*. Now I shall describe the ritual placement (*nyāsa*); one should indeed perform the placement of the pure *Mātṛkā*. Brahmā is declared its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *Gāyatrī* is said to be its meter (*chandas*), and the deity is Mātṛkā; one should place the seed-syllable (*bīja*) as "Ha" and the power (*śakti*) as "Kṣa," which is called the Supreme. The application (*niyoga*) grants all accomplishments. Having performed the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should carry out the placement as before: on the head, the mouth, the eyes, the ears, the two nostrils, the cheeks, the lips, the teeth, the tip of the tongue, and the region of the throat. One should place the letters from Ka onwards on the right hand, and the Ca-group on the left.

One should place the *ṭa*-group on the right hand and the *ta*-group on the left foot. One should place the five letters beginning with *gha* (*gha-ṅa*) on the sides, the back, the navel, and the belly. The bodily constituents (*dhātus*) are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of these along with the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the supreme soul (*paramātman*), while recollecting the *Yāvī* [mantra] in sequence. One should place the letter *ca* on the heart, *cha* on the right shoulder, and *ja* on the left shoulder. Afterwards, from the hands down to the feet and up to the head—from the head down to the feet—the best of practitioners should perform the placement in the order of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*), starting from the letter *kṣa* and ending with the letter *a*. [The placement of] the letter *ḍa*...

O Mistress of the Kula, I shall now describe the unsurpassed placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters ending in *ṭ*, as declared in the scriptures. The Seer (*ṛṣi*) is Nāgaṣṭimūrti, whose nature is to agitate the unshakeable; the meter (*chaṃdas*) is known as *Paṅkti*, and the application (*viniyoga*) bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). Having uttered the *Tāra* (Om), O Goddess of Gods, one should say "Salutation, salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*). Then one should utter the syllable *hrīṃ* and place it on the Head (*śiras*) with the beloved of Fire (Svāhā). Having uttered the syllable *strīṃ*, one should place it at the end of the Crest-lock (*śikhā*) with *vaṣaṭ*. With the Armor mantra (*varma*), O Goddess, one should again place it upon the Body (*tanu*). Having uttered the Weapon mantra (*astra*), one should again place it upon the three Eyes (*netratraya*).

The wise one should place [the seed-syllables] and then utter the *vahnijāyā* (the consort of fire, *svāhā*). After the *astra-mantra*, he should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) and then establish the conch (*śaṅkha*). He should worship with the *astra-mantra* and the ground, and the wise one should draw a triangle.

First, he should extract the *vāgbhava* (AIM) preceded by the *ādhāra-mantra*. O Great Goddess, he should cast the *māyāvīja* (HŪM) into the great conch. He should worship the great petal [of the lotus], which is mounted upon the moon, the sixth vowel (Ū), adorned with the left eye (I), and pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. He should cast the flowers of the *mahāvīrakrama-latā-vajra*. He should purify the substance with the *mūla-mantra* and protect it with the *astra-mantra*.

One should worship the veil with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and thereafter display the *yonimudrā*. Having recited the garland of letters (*varṇamālā*) in both ascending and descending order, and having performed meditation upon Tāriṇī, the supreme power (*paramā kalā*), O Maheśānī, one should then perform the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*) and contemplate the state of the deity. Having raised Kuṇḍalinī, who is garlanded with the fifty letters, one should begin the meditation within the triangle in the great lotus of the *mūlādhāra*. Meditating on her as being of red color, one should hold her above the heart. One should worship the Great Goddess, who is blue in color and holds a sword and a skull-bowl, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

One should cause it to enter through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and meditate upon the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā* as raining down streams of nectar. Having meditated upon that which consists of consciousness and bliss, and having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) according to the rules and offer it into the left hand of the deity.

[Thus ends the third chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. Now I shall describe the worship of the Dūtī, who carries one across the difficult-to-cross [ocean of existence], who stands on the shore of the subtle [reality], and who is skilled in the secret ear-tradition of the Kula. She is a young woman of sixteen years, with full and elevated breasts, intoxicated like a rutting elephant, her eyes rolling from passion, and possessing the eyes of a fawn.

[He should worship] the lady with beautiful eyes, soft-smiling, free from anger, greed, shame, pride, delusion, and deceit, always delighted in the dharma of her lord, truthful, ever-pure, whether she be a Maṇikā, a Caṇḍālī, a Pācakī, or the wife of a lover; one whose limbs bear the *yogamudrā*, a tanner, or a weaver; endowed with the four castes, most excellent, born of the mountains; embracing [the Lord] on his left side. [The practitioner should draw] a triangle, a lotus, and a circle, joined with white and red, and smeared with blue and vermilion. The practitioner, facing east, should worship the Goddess who faces west. Pī...
One should worship the nine Śaktis by means of the eight-fold ritual (aṣṭa-śakti-vidhāna). These nine Śaktis are Prīti, Priyā, Kānti, Kāminī, Kāmamālinī, Kaṃdarpadalinī, Durgā, and Bhavānī.

Having uttered the syllable *viyat* (the sky, *ha*) and *bhṛgu* (the sage, *sa*), followed by the mantra (*ma*) endowed with the bindu (*m*) and the digit (*kalā*, *ī*), then the word *mahāpreta* (Great Preta), and finally the word *dhṛta* (held) ending in *yam*—this is the mantra. Having recited the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) followed by the vocative form of the word *Tāriṇī*, then the words *ehy ehi ca* (come, come), and again and again the words *pādukābhyām* (by the sandals), one should take [her] with the left hand and seat her upon the throne. Her limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, she is adorned with red flowers, and she is equipped with all ornaments.

One should worship her as she is joined [with the consort], naked, holding wine in her hand, and filled with the sentiment of erotic play (*hāva-bhāva*). One should cause her to drink until she reaches the level of her throat. One should perform meditation thus:

"O Mistress, O you with the cavernous mouth and the face of an elephant, whose form is like the crest of a cock—O Goddess, one should contemplate you, the Vidyā who deludes the world, stationed there.

Then, from the syllable *Tāra* (Om) up to the end of the heart-mantra, followed by the temple of Madana (Kāmadeva), one should worship the Goddess using the vocative case endings and cast flowers into the *bhaga*. Having stirred it with the *Kulagrantha*, one should offer perfumes and flowers.

One should mark [the body] and, having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should thereafter worship the ornaments. After that, one should worship the deities Dhatrī, Tānā, Kriyā, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Cārurudrikā, Rati, Prīti, and Kāma, as well as the one who holds the flower-arrows and bow, and Vasantas. Then, O Goddess, one should worship the Maṃtra-kurasa along with Cikura.
One should worship Viriñci at the navel and Hara-Hari at the heart. O Maheśānī, during the bathing and dressing, one should then worship Trimūrti. One should worship Kāma in the Mānā-tukāma.

One should worship the five arrows at the root of the *Śīparā-tu-bhaga-mālinī* and the *Bhuvaumaheśānī*. One should utter *Drām* and so forth for *Drāviṇī* in the mouth; one should say *Drīm* for *Kṣobhiṇī*; *Klīṃ* for "attract" (*ākarṣaya*) and *Klūṃ* for "delusion" (*saṃmohana*). The five arrows are declared to end with the letter *Sa* and the *visarga*. One should worship the *śakti* on the two ears in the order of the sun and the moon. Having worshipped Fire (*vahni*) on the tongue, one should worship *Nakṣatramālinī* in the eyes. One should worship *Prāṇa* in the nose and *Tripathagāminī* in the *ājñā* [cakra].

One should worship Akṣobhya on the crown of the head with offerings of perfumes and flowers; one should place a garland of flowers around the neck and then the wise person should recite [the mantra] according to their capacity. Now I shall explain the ritual placement (nyāsa): one should meditate upon Śiva within oneself and perform the placement in sequence upon the five faces of Mahādeva, endowed with his kalās. First, "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" [is the mantra for the face], and "Śaśinī" is the first kalā. Next, "Īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām," followed by "Aṅgada. Then, at the end of the word "Brahmādhipati," [one places] "Brahmaṇo'dhipatiṃ" again. Then, "Brahma" and finally, "Śivo me'stu."

One should place the *Ṛic* in the form of a casket (*sampuṭa*), having first uttered "Sadāśivoṃ. Then follows another, "Aṃśumān. "O Goddess, one should place [the mantra] in the heart in sequence: 'Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe' is the *Kala* called *Śānti*; 'Mahādevāya dhīmahi' is likewise the *Kala* called *Vidyā*; then the word 'Tanno Rudraḥ' is said to be the *Kala* called *Pratiṣṭhā*; and after uttering 'Pracodayāt', there is the *Kala* called *Nivṛtti*. [Then] in the east, west, south, and north respectively, O Goddess, one should place [the mantra] in the heart: 'Aghorebhyo' [is for the head], and from delusion (moha) [one places it] on the neck."

One should place *Ghorā* on the back; then one should place *Kriyā* on the right shoulder. Then one should place *Nidrā* on the left shoulder with the mantra *Ghoratarebhyaḥ*. Having uttered *Sarva* everywhere, one should place *Vyādhi* on the navel. One should place *Sakalā* on the region of the belly with the mantra *Sarvebhyaḥ*. Then, following the sequence of the limbs (*parokramāt*), one should place *Sudhā* on the back with *Namaste*, and *Kalā* with *Rudrarūpebhyaḥ*. One should place *Tṛṣā* at the end with *Tyinamoṃtakaḥ*. One should place *Rajas* at the secret parts with *Vāmadevāya namoṃte*. One should place *Rakṣā* on the testicles with *Bhejyeṣṭhāya*. One should place *Arati* with *Rudrāya namoḥ*.

One should assign *Ścādvāmamuṣkekalā* with the mantra "Obeisance to Kālāyana" to the right testicle; O Lord of Devas, one should assign *Pālinī* and *Vāmā* to the left with "Obeisance to Kiraṇa. Having uttered the word "Obeisance," one should assign *Saṃyuminī* to the right knee. Having uttered *Valā* and then *Vṛddhi*, one should assign [the deity] to the right buttock. One should assign *Prathamā* and *Rātri* to the left buttock. Having uttered "Obeisance" at the end of "to the Subduer of All Beings" (*sarvabhūtadamana*), one should assign the digit *Kaṅmaṇī* to the region of the hips. Having uttered "Obeisance" at the end, one should assign the great digit (*mahatīkalā*) to the right side.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), ending in the dative case, and concluding with "namaḥ. Having performed this rite of placement (*nyāsa*), one should contemplate oneself as Śiva, intent upon the meditation on Rudra while keeping the five-syllabled mantra foremost. Having meditated upon the deity as consisting of the essence of the *sāmaveda*, one should recite the armor (*kavaca*) for the sake of protection. Having bound the *kṣobhiṇī-mudrā*, one should cast the yantra into the center. One should cause the goddess *drāviṇī* to melt and extract the great *caitanya* (consciousness) by means of the *latā*. Having released the *yonimudrā*, one should cast it into the *kunayā*; the wise man [should then place] the *bhaga*.

Having uttered the *liṅga*, the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *vīryaka* along with all the *talas*, one should perform a recitation (*japa*) of a thousand times. One should worship the nine *pīṭha-śaktis*, beginning with Vāmā, according to the prescribed rule. On the eight petals starting from the east, one should worship the goddess Sarasvatī; likewise, one should worship Rati, Prīti, Kānti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and the eighth goddess, Prajñā, in the center. In the manner previously described, one should worship the great *mahāpreta-āsana*. At the end of the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should utter the unsurpassed *pīṭha-mantra* of the goddess. Having invoked the seed-syllable (*bīja*) therein, one should worship the three powers (*triśakti*).

One should perform meditation according to the prescribed rite upon Tāriṇī, the savior from fear. She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, possesses three eyes, and utters fierce *aṭṭahāsa* laughter. Her arms hold a sword, a blue lotus, a flaying knife (*kartṛ*), and a skull-cup (*kapāla*). Born from the seed-syllable *Hūṃ*, she is short and her matted locks are dark, wide, and tawny, bound by fierce serpents. In the skull placed upon her head, she destroys the dullness of the three worlds. Today, one should meditate on Ugratārā: standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture with her foot placed upon the heart of a corpse; possessing the luster of crystal, blazing, and dark blue; wearing a garland of deep blue lotuses; with rays of reddish light, a flickering tongue, and a terrifying countenance; [and] risen... (unmatta).

One should worship the Goddess on the sacred seat after meditating upon her thus: she who is intoxicated with passion, whose thighs are stout from the internal intoxication, whose limbs are slender, who possesses the five mudrās, who is exceedingly sweet like wine, whose eyes are rolling, whose arms are adorned with a sword, a blue lotus, a blade, and a skull-bowl, who is born from the fierce *kapila* fire, whose matted hair is bound by the lord of serpents, who drinks honey-wine, who is beautiful with garlands of severed heads, who is clothed in the directions of space, who wears a garland of wild beasts, who utters the sounds "Daha Daha Daha Gaṃ" and laughs with loud, boisterous laughter—may that Dākṣī, the mother of the gods, whose form is liberation even in sexual union, protect me. Having meditated in this way, one should offer three handfuls of flowers to the Goddess on the seat.

One should offer a welcome, inquire after their welfare, and display the nine mudrās. Having recited the root mantra (mūlamantra) and awakened one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should utter the word "Bhagavatī" for the Goddess who dwells within all.

Then, at the end of the mantra "parikalpayāmi," one should say "hṛdayānte. After that, the practitioner should again offer a handful of flowers with the root mantra. One should offer water for the feet (pādya) at the feet, and then speak the *argha* mantra once more. O Maheśānī, one should offer the *argha* with the head [of the mantra] using the "Vahni-vallabhā" [mantra]. Afterwards, one should say "ācamanīya" and "svadhā" for the mouth.

After that, one should utter the word "dhūpam" (incense) at the end of the *hṛdaya* mantra, and then the *mantra* again; one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) separately for each *mantra*. One should present the offerings such as food (*naivedya*) along with sandalwood paste and other services.

As for the food offering, one should give blood together with meat and other such items. One should offer three handfuls of flowers and recite the *mantra* according to one's capacity. Having finished the recitation, one should perform the offering (*samarpaṇa*) into the left hand of the deity. [Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. Having invoked [the deity], one should worship it, beginning with its limbs and along with the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇas*), within the center of the *bindu*.

One should worship Heśāni and Triśakti; then one should worship the couple consisting of Rati, Prīti, Priyā, and Kānti, who bear the flower-arrows and the bow. Afterward, one should meditate upon Gāyatrī and Caturānana (Brahmā), and worship Sāvitrī and the deity Viṣṇu. Having invoked Vāgīśvarī, one should worship Rudra and Maithuna. O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship the Guru and Akṣobhya in the form of a row. Afterward, one should worship Kartṛkā and worship Citāṅgāra. O Goddess, one should worship the six limbs within the hexagon and satisfy the ancestors.

One should utter the name of each [deity] preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and followed by the word *vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha*, ending with *svāhā*. I shall now declare their names in their respective places in due order. One should worship the goddess on the petals in the four directions, starting from the east: in the east, the one named Vairocana; then in the north, Asitāṅga; in the west, the one called Padmanābha; and in the south, Śaṅkhapāṇḍura. Afterwards, one should worship in the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast corner in sequence: Nāmaka, Māmaka, Pāṇḍara, and Nara.

The practitioner should everywhere address the name with a vocative particle and perform worship at the four gates, starting with Padmāntaka and the others in sequence. Having worshipped Sūrya in the center, he should then worship the lineage of the Guru. He should worship the other deities, Rudra, and then worship the Goddess again. The wise one should offer three handfuls of flowers and recite the mantra according to the prescribed number. He should perform the *samarpaṇa* (offering) to Lakṣmī and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the crest and limbs. Having worshipped with the six limbs, he should consecrate [the disciple] with the root mantra. He should perform [the rite] upon the body of the divine disciple with the root mantra.

In the four-petaled lotus of Lādhā, within the stainless triangle, one should perform the meditation on the divine Creative Will (Cit-kriyā). One should meditate upon the Goddess who consists of Śiva and Śakti, whose form is pure consciousness alone, who is entwined with the creeper of the three folds, and who possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns. With a body as slender as a lotus fiber, this Goddess pierces through the sequence of the six wheels; moving by way of the central path (madhyamā), she proceeds as far as the supreme Śiva. One should withdraw the vowels from *v* to *s* and assign them to the six petals. One should contemplate the consonants from *va* to *la* and pierce the imperishable Guru. One should then withdraw those phonemes.

O Viṣṇu, having joined those ten syllables again in the jewel-lotus, one should join those syllables in the heart. Surrounded by the Rudras, one should join the letters from *ka* to *ṅa* in the heart; then, withdrawing those syllables, the practitioner should join them in the throat-lotus. In the Viśuddha [chakra], the practitioner should join the sixteen vowels. Then, having withdrawn them along with Śiva, he should join them again in the command-lotus (*ājñā-saroruha*) which has two petals and is endowed with syllables. Having joined the Guru there, one should withdraw him with those syllables and join him up to the digit (*kalā*) in the eye.
Having joined [the disciple] with Lāṃ, Nāda, and Anaṅga, the best of teachers should join him with Unmanī. He should join Unmattā within the space between the Viṣṇu-cakra and the Moon.

Having again joined her to the mouth, the supreme teacher should pierce the Śakti together with the Self (ātman). At that very moment, the disciple, having become the form of the deity, speaks everything.
O Maheśānī, O Kuleśvarī, he should place the vessel in the hand of the disciple, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, and after bowing, ask for forgiveness according to his means.

Then, one should satisfy [the deity] according to one's capacity; having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should offer garments, ornaments, elephants, wealth, grain, various jewels, and land to the Guru for the sake of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. [Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. Now, I shall explain the extraction of the mantra of Vakreśānī:
Tārā, Ekajaṭā, Nīlā, Triśakti, Eka-sādhinī, Haṃsarūpā, Mahātārā, Siddhakālī—this is the twofold mantra. [Also] Padmāvatī, Mahādevī, Mahānīla...

Sarasvatī, Jalāyachamanī, Tārā, the bestower of all accomplishments, Mahācainakramā, Devī, Tāriṇī, and the leader of mantras—these are proclaimed as the thirteen Great Vidyās of Tārā. That Kālī who is Mahātārā is remembered as Tārākālikā; through a sense of distinction between these two, the loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs. In the south, Mahākālī is proclaimed to have nine divisions (*bhedas*), while forty-eight divisions of Chinnā are proclaimed. Yogeśvarī, Mahādevī, Aṅgirā, and the threefold mantra [are also included].

This Great Vidyā of Tārā bestows fruits upon the worlds. Having first extracted *Tāram* (the syllable Om), one should extract the seed-syllable *Hṛllekhā*. Joined with *Bhṛgu* (S), *Ākhaṇḍa* (A), and half of that which consists of fire (R)—that is, the letter *Ra*—it is joined with the left eye (I) and adorned with the Bindu and Nāda. Then there is the Moon (U), the Lord of Serpents (M), and the letter for worship at the beginning. Adorned with the Bindu, Nāda, Kalā, and Kāra, and further embellished by the left eye (I), this is the King of Mantras, O Maheśānī, another mantra difficult to obtain. I shall now proclaim the *Kullukā-mantra*, for the practitioner is indeed the Lord of the Kula: having uttered *Viyat* (H), *Vahni* (R), and the left eye (I).

One should place the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, preceded by the Bindu and mounted upon the Bhṛgu-vajra (the letter *B*), combined with the Unstable-Eyed One (*Ulolākṣī*) and the Bindu. Having placed this supreme seed-mantra of Lakṣmī, which bestows the accomplishment of night and is the root-vidyā of the three abodes in union with Māyā, one should first extract the Praṇava (*Oṃ*), then extract the seed-mantra Hṛllekhā (*Hrīṃ*). After that, the word "To Vaṭuka" (*Vaṭukāya*) for the removal of calamities; then, having uttered "Do [this] twice" (*Kuru Kuru*), one should extract Māyā (*Hrīṃ*) and Tāra (*Oṃ*). This mantra, joined with the Fire-born Consort (*Svāhā*), should offer the oblation to Vaṭuka in the south-east.

One should utter *lim utsṛjya māyā-lakṣmīś ca manmathaḥ*. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Vārāhī, one should again utter the seed-syllable of Pañcānana (*pañcānaka*). Then the word *gaṇapataye*, followed by *varavarada*, and then *sarvajana* and likewise *śam ānaya*. At the end, one should add the consort of Fire (*vahnivadhū*); this is the great mantra of Gaṇanātha. Having extracted the Raudra syllable three times, one should then utter Nārāyaṇa. Having extracted the seed-syllable of Sūkṣmeśa, one should extract the seed-syllable of Amareśa. Then one should utter *ṅentaṃ kṣetrapālaṃ tu valiṃ gṛhṇa* twice.

The mantra of Kṣetrapāla, joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-seed *ra*), is a great mantra. Having written the seed-syllable of Vāyu (*ya*) three times, [followed by] Ananta, Mādhava, and [the rest], if each is joined individually, it bestows its respective fruit; this knowledge (*vidyā*) that grants the four aims of life is remembered as Ekajaṭā. Joined with Viyat (space, *ha*) and Bindu (*m*), Bhṛgu (the seed *bha*) conjoined with Sarga (the visarga *ḥ*), then Candra (the moon, *sa*) ending with Bhautika (the letter *va*), and finally Candra (*sa*) joined with Bindu (*m*): O fair-limbed one, this knowledge is proclaimed as Haṃsatārā. At the beginning, [one should place] Tāra (the syllable *oṃ*) joined with Śiva (the letter *ha*) and Śakti (the letter *au*).

One should extract [the seed-syllable] joined with the Bindu (ṃ) and Sarga (ḥ); that is the first, and below it [is the second], in due order. This is declared to be the Haṃsa-mantra, beginning with Māyā (Hrīṃ) and ending with the seed-syllable of the Armor (Huṃ). This eight-syllabled Vidyā bestows the sovereignty of knowledge. Then again: Vāgbhava (Aiṃ), the seed-syllable of the Armor (Huṃ), the speech of Sadyojāta (Ha), Māyā (Hrīṃ), and the Astra (Phaṭ) ending with Dviṭha (Svāhā)—this is the mantra of Kālikā.

O lady of excellent hips, this is the Siddhividyā, the eight-syllabled Vidyā of Sāraṅgī. First extracting Tāra (Oṃ), then Lohita (Ra) and Mīna (I), joined with Jayā (E) and Ekadaśa (Na)—and once again...

One should likewise utter the word *mahāpadme*, followed by the word *padmāvatī*. Then there are two syllables ending with two *ga*s, [the letter] *ya*, and *uddha-darśana-śālinī*. This is the goddess Padmāvatī, consisting of seventeen syllables. A wise man should perform the recitation (*japa*) of this mantra at midnight at a crossroads; he will obtain great power of poetic composition—of this there is no doubt. The seed-syllable at the end of speech (*vāk-lajjā*), then *Pinākī* and *Śambhu*, along with *Bhṛgu*, endowed with the fourteenth vowel (*au*), adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, joined with the moon (*ca*) and space (*ha*), and likewise with *anugraha* (*ai*) and *īśa* (*ha*).

The mantra consists of thirty-four syllables: *visagaṃ* (ḥ), the two words *tipada* and *dvadva*, the word *pada*, the word *vāgvādinī* repeated twice, the word *nīlā*, the word *punarnīlā*, one should then utter *sarasvatī*, *vāṅmāyāṃ*, followed by the pair of words *kuha-śaśa*, then *kamalāṃ* and *vahnijāyāṃ* (svāhā). This mantra is to be understood as being applied to the six corners in both direct and reverse order. The Seer (*ṛṣi*) is Janārdana, whose form is the flood of the Gaṅgā;
the metre (*chandas*) is Atyantāvākavitā; the Goddess is Nīlasarasvatī; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Vāgbhava (aiṃ); the power (*śakti*) is Māyā (hrīṃ); and the pillar (*kīlaka*) is Lakṣmī (śrīṃ).

The fruit of the lack of poetic skill has been declared; I worship the fierce Sarasvatī, who holds four arms, who is gentle, who is distinguished by playing the lute, who smiles with the lotus-like faces of the Gaṇas, who holds a jar rich in nectar in her left hand, and who displays the supreme mudrā in her other hand. For one who thus worships the goddess Mahānīla-Sarasvatī, his speech consisting of prose and verse flows like the current of the Gaṅgā.

Through the yoga of meditation for six months, he is sung of along with the Kinnaras. Having written the two [syllables] of the sky (ha-kāra and sa-kāra) with a bindu upon the left ear, then the three qualities (guṇa), then the Raudra [seed-syllable], and then Brahmā...

One should extract the *nīvīja* (the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu), then write the *māheśī-bīja* (the seed-syllable of Maheśī). This five-syllabled great mantra (*pañcākṣara-mahāmanu*) bestows all prosperity. A wise person should assign the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs] as before, and then assign this *pūrvatāriṇī*. One should employ it in the station of the five rays and utter "Tāre" after each "Tāre. This is the water-born *tārā*, ending with "Viṭhām," consisting of twelve syllables.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the number of its syllables, and perform oblations (*homa*) with one-tenth that amount, using red flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), either in a cremation ground, at a crossroads, or in an empty temple.
At night, the wise should perform the worship of her who is blue-colored, three-eyed, two-armed, seated upon a lotus, served by hosts of gods, with a smiling countenance and red ornaments;

she is endowed with youth, possesses full and elevated breasts, and has her pair of lotus-feet placed upon jeweled sandals—to her I offer my salutation. For all these vidyās, one should perform everything as previously described.

Having uttered the *tāra* (Om) and *māyā* (Hrīṃ), one should extract the remainder, "Viyat" (Ha). Then one should say, "She who enables one to cross over all calamities difficult to overcome. This mantra consists of twelve, two, four, and four syllables respectively. It is auspicious.

One should recite the *Rapa-dadapa* mantra four hundred thousand times; indeed, for such a person, the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arise. One should perform meditation and worship for this mantra just as one does for the five-syllabled mantra. [Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*. Now I shall fully explain the supreme *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary observance). For one who is devoid of *puraścaraṇa*, the perfection of the mantra does not occur. First, one should perform the *puraskriyā* according to rule and in accordance with the prescribed method. The wise practitioner should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and offer oblations (*homa*) ten times that amount (forty thousand) using lotuses mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhura*). Such a person becomes a master of speech. [End of section on the sacred field.]

Having purified the area with cow dung and water along with the thread, one should have an altar constructed there; in its center, one should place a skull. One should perform an anointing with honey and draw an eight-petaled lotus in the middle.

One should write the pairs of vowels in order starting from the east, and there one should write the eight groups of consonants (*vargāṣṭaka*). In the center, one should draw the *Prāsāda* mantra. Likewise, O beautiful lady, one should write the *Gagana* (Ha) joined with the *Bindu*, as well as *Lāṅgalīśa* (Sa) with the *Visarga*, in the filaments. Having worshipped the *Ādhāra* and other elements there, the wise man should prepare a seat. Having sat upon that seat, the hero may remain wherever he is.

In the *pyacūlaka* [mudrā], one should perform three strikes with the heels and then three snaps of the fingers. The preceptor should then perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the weapon-rite (*astrakarma*) starting from the east in due order, using the Astra-mantra. Having uttered the word "Paśu" at the end of the corpse's hair—[the syllable] adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*, ending with the armor (*varma*), and followed by the unsurpassed Astra-mantra—this is the Vidyā known as Pāśupata, which destroys all obstacles.

Then, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) according to the rules, preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and having assigned the seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), and other attributes, one should offer oblations (*bali*) to the deities of the directions. Asitāṅga-Bhairava [is the lord of the east]; [one should worship] Brāhmī... [the rest of the verse follows].

One should draw the enclosure and perform the ritual for grasping the boundary; the mantra for the boundary of the directions ends with *viṭhānta*. The eight Bhairavas are Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta-Bhairava, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra. Then follow Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and thereafter she who is known as Mahālakṣmī, in sequence beginning with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*). Having worshipped them thoroughly with incense and lamps, one should subsequently fix the ritual stake (*kīla*). First, having uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), [the mantra is] Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Manmatha, [followed by] "to Indrāṇī."

Having uttered the word *Cāmuṇḍe*, then the word *viśve*, and afterwards the phrase *idaṃ kṣetraṃ kīlaya*, one should then write the words *rakṣa rakṣa* followed by *kīlake*. This mantra ends with the *vahnijāyā* (the fire-born wife, *svāhā*). One should worship it according to the sequence starting from the east. Having fully recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should utter the word *āgneyī*; then the word *yāmyai*, then again the mantra for *naiṛtyai*; then *vāruṇyai*, *vāpavī*, *kauverī*, *īśānabhairavī*. Having first fully recited the mantra, one should then speak the name of the Goddess and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) in due order.

One should offer oblations (bali) in the two intermediate directions. First, having extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should extract the seed-syllable Hṛllekhā (Hrīṃ). Then the word "Vaṭukāya," followed by "for the removal of calamities" (āpaduddhāraṇāya). Having uttered "do it" (kuru) twice, one should extract the Tāra (Oṃ) along with Māyā (Hrīṃ). This mantra, joined with Vahnijāyā (Svāhā), is for offering the oblation to Vaṭuka. Having offered the oblation in the south-east, one should [utter]: Māyā (Hrīṃ), Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), and Manmatha (Klīṃ); then extract the seed-syllable of Vārāhī (Hrūṃ), and again the fifty-fold seed-syllable (the fifty letters of the alphabet). Then the word "Gaṇapataye," followed by "Varavarada" (bestower of boons), and again... Sa.

And likewise, one should cause the entire kingdom to be pacified. At the end, one should offer the bride to the Fire; this is the great mantra of Gaṇanātha. Having extracted the Raudra mantra three times, one should utter Nārāyaṇa. Having extracted the seed-mantra Sūkṣma, one should extract the seed-mantra of Amareśa. Then, having uttered "Ṅentaṃ tu Kṣetrapāla" and "Baliṃ gṛhṇa" twice, followed by the wife of Fire (Svāhā), this is the great mantra of Kṣetrapāla. Having written the seed-mantra of Vāyu three times, then Ananta and Mādhava, and then having taken Vartulākṣī, likewise for the Yoginīs, followed by the wife of Fire—this is the Yoginī mantra for the northwest.

One should extract the syllable *vali* (va-li) mounted upon the letter *kṣa*, followed at its end by the fire-syllable (*ra*)—which creates the state of all obstacles—and then extract *sarvebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ* (to all beings). After this, one should extract *varma* (huṃ), followed by *phaṭ*, and then say *valiṃ gṛhṇāpaya*. This mantra, ending with *svāhā* (dviṭha), is declared to be the bestower of success; with it, one should offer the oblation (*vali*) to all beings. The offerings consist of rice, milk-porridge (*pāyasa*), milk, fish, meat, likewise sweetmeats (*modaka*), fried cakes (*pūrikā*), clarified butter (*pūya*), fritters (*vaṭaka*), the three types of liquor, curd-rice, cooked food, ghee, and curd with sugar. One should perform all these according to the prescribed rules and should not perform the ritual casting away of the milk. On ground smeared with cow dung, one should draw a mandala.

One should apply the paste of *alīna* and glowing clay. A lotus marked by a thread, with even lines and captivating, red, white, green, and black petals and beautiful filaments, should be fashioned; it is square, richly adorned, and in its center is a pair of *yoni*s. In the middle of that is a triangle, and within that, one should contemplate the Void within the Void. One should join the channels (*nāḍī*s) there and unite the mantra. Having established her right there, O Goddess—she who is slightly smiling, with beautiful eyes, a sixteen-year-old maiden, not yet having borne a child, ascetic, wearing clean garments under her own control, fearless, and laughing loudly—[one should proceed].

One should worship such a woman at the time of the vigil—one who possesses intense intellect, firm conduct, loose hair, and is naked or clad in the garments of yoga, being solely devoted to the path of Yoga—while joined with the mantra. She may be a Mātaṅgī, a Naṭukārī, a Vāmārthī, a Bhītināśinī, a Ṣaṭkārī, a Carmakārī, a Chipinī, or one born of a Nāpita; she may especially be a woman from the market (Haṭṭanārī) who is delicate and strewn with her own flowers.

One should place the general *arghya*, the special *arghya*, one's own vessel, and the vessel of power (*śaktipātra*) there, and within them, one should pour the substance produced from the nectar of union. A wise person should purify each of these individually with the mantra of the five principles (*tatva*).

At the end of the digit of Fire (Ra), the Sun (Re), and the Moon (Ca), one should write the Heart-mantra (Hrīm) within a triangle. In the center of that triangle, one should write the syllables beginning with A, ending with Kha (Ka), followed by Pha, Ananta (Ha), Bha, and Dha, joined with the letter Śa and the letter Ga (Śaga).

This should be adorned with the left ear (Ū), the Bindu, and the Nāda. This is the mantra consisting of the five jewels, renowned as Ratneśvarī. One should worship it with the six limbs and consecrate it with the root mantra. Then, one should perform the internal sacrifice oneself as Mahogratāriṇī. Having raised Kuṇḍalinī, who traverses the three paths, to the "three-footed" place, one fills the life-channel (Prāṇanāḍī); there, the emergence of the Sound (Nāda) occurs. Nā...

One should contemplate the *arghya* (offering water) produced from the moon there, shaped like a *kadamba* bud, consisting of the movement within the void, the essence of Śiva and Śakti, and having the nature of a stream of nectar.

Then, one should contemplate the Supreme Śiva, both manifest and unmanifest, arisen from the *nāda*, the Great Buddha born therein, the source, the ultimate refuge. One should display the *mudrās* to Him—the *Śṛgī*, the *Haṃsī*, and the *Vajriṇī*. O Goddess, one should satisfy Him three times with [offerings] upon each of His heads. One should contemplate a triangle on the head, proceeding in order from south to north; the mantras are Vyomakeśa, Uddhakeśa, and Nīlakaṇṭha. [And] Nandā...

One should worship that [deity] afterwards; first, one should worship Vyomā. Likewise, one should worship Urdhvakeśa and Nīla in Divyaughā. Having meditated upon the radiant Śakti and worshipped Ugratāriṇī, one should worship Tāra, Māyā, Varma, and the three Tārās at the beginning. One should worship Matsya, Kūrma, Vasiṣṭha, Maheśvara, Ānanda, Tārā, Bhānumatī, Jayā, Vidyā, Mahodarī, and Avāntā in the center. From the perspective of the state of being, Ekajaya and Śivā are to be known as belonging to the Siddhaugha according to the lineage of the traditional gurus. [He is] the giver of bliss.

Parānanda, Pārijātakuleśvara, Virūpākṣa, and likewise Bhīma; having joined these with "Bhairava" and "Mānavodhata," one should recite the mantra ending in "Namaḥ. Having worshipped the row [of letters] on the head, and having satiated the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti at the Mūlādhāra with one's own name according to the designation of the five mudrās—namely *ali* (wine), *piśita* (meat), *mīna* (fish), the supreme *mudrā* (sexual union), and *maithuna* (copulation)—the Goddess is undoubtedly present wherever those five "Ma"s are found. There is no wine that is not *mādhavī-madya* (liquor made from *mādhavī* flowers); wine arises from the essence of power (*śakti*). *Sukhuṇḍa*, *śaṅkhinī*, *matsya*, *mudrā*, and the supreme *unmatta* are the essence of Soma.

O Sadāśiva, sexual union is of three kinds: divine (*divya*), heroic (*vīra*), and animal (*paśu*); likewise, drinking is also of three types. A hero who delights in animal drinking is a consumer [of flesh] along with the hosts of Yoginīs. A hero who delights in divine drinking attains union (*sāyujya*) with the Goddess. Through heroic drinking, the Guru goes to the world of the Goddess; through animal drinking, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) shall go to the Raurava hell. Prāṇāyāma, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the consumption of the corpse (*śavāhāra*), and the purification of the mind—having pierced the solar orb and entered the center of the lunar orb, one should always [proceed] by way of the path of Suṣumṇā.

This divine drink (*divyapāna*), which pours down like a continuous stream, is said to bestow all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). Having set aside all worldly attachments and being pure at the root of one's being, one should satisfy [the deities] through the five principles (*pañcatattva*) in accordance with worldly conduct. Through the sequential yoga of the six chakras, one should offer the substance accompanied by mantras. This supreme *vīrapāna* consists of the state of meditation, worship, and transcendence. One who is attached and greedy, hypocritical, lacking conviction in the meaning of the mantra, lustful, or devoid of desire—such a person is called a *paśu* (bound soul) regarding the drink. [Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. Perform the worship as before.

Having worshipped this Yantra together with its limbs (aṅgas) and enclosures (āvaraṇas) using perfumes and flowers, one should thereafter perform the recitation (japa). Having properly performed his daily rites, being well-bathed and intent upon his vow, with his soul absorbed in the Guru and the Mantra, eating only at night and remaining pure by day, he should perform worship at night; he should worship with creeper-flowers. The wise man should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number.
He should especially and diligently perform the homa in a Yoni-kunda. For all undertakings, milk-rice (pāyasa) yields the best results, as does the homa of blue lotuses (nīlotpala).

By offering heart-pleasing flowers (*hṛdyāri-kusuma*), a man becomes a lord; all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*) arise from this. By an oblation of *japā* flowers, a deer-eyed woman is brought under control. With *mālatī*, great wisdom is attained; with *kadamba* flowers, there is the cheating of Death (*kālavañcana*). With red lotuses (*raktotpala*), great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*) is gained; for the purpose of paralyzing (*staṃbhana*), one should offer *campaka* flowers. One should offer beautiful leaves of the *bilva* tree for rites of pacification (*śāntikarma*). By an oblation of sesame seeds (*tilahoma*), one is liberated from all sins. Through an oblation of *dūrvā* grass, one gains long life; with *vetasa* reeds, one becomes a giver of rain. One should perform the oblation eight times with coconuts (*nālikera*).

The practitioner shall obtain stable fortune, like a king followed by his attendants; by the homa of plantain fruit, the Goddess is satisfied instantly. With *ātuluṅga* (citron) comes the attainment of desires, and with *vibhītaka* or *nimba*, one slays the enemy in an instant. For the rite of *māraṇa* (killing) or *abhicāra* (sorcery), these substances are prescribed: mustard seed, *rājila* (a type of snake), salt, black pepper, asafoetida, and *arka-ja* (the product of the *arka* tree). Each fruit, flower, and so forth, as well as grapes (*drākṣā*)—five of each—is prescribed; likewise, *guggulu* equal to a *badarī* fruit, and *kapittha* is remembered as being of two kinds [in measure], four...
One *pala* of mature *mātuluṅga*, one *mārīci* (black pepper) in measure, *caṃdracora* (camphor), saffron, mustard seed, and *rājika* (black mustard) each in the measure of thirty-two *tuṣas*;

one *karṣa* of salt, four *guñjās* of *hiṅgu* (asafetida), one *karṣa* of ghee—which is called "divine milk"—one *śukti* of curd, one *pala* of *dhānyaka* (coriander), three blades of *dūrvā* grass, and twelve finger-breadths of *vetasa* (willow); all these, when combined with the three sweets (*trimadhura*) for the accomplishment of pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and so forth, and when combined with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) for the rites of killing (*māraṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and the like.

One should offer ten thousand oblations in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using the flesh of a boar, a deer, a goat, or a buffalo; one will then become like Vaiśravaṇa in wealth. For the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), it is taught that the fruit [is obtained] by offering the flesh of a dove, a vulture, an owl, as well as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), a cock, and a jackal. One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) according to the rules with the prescribed number of substances, using either honey, clarified butter, wine, or water.
The master of the great mantra should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). On ground smeared with cow dung, one should draw a lotus petal and place a water-pot (*kalaśa*).

One should establish the *kalā* there and worship it with perfumes, *dūrvā* sprouts, *aśoka* flowers, and mango shoots. Having worshipped with offerings such as perfumes and flowers, one should worship [the deity] while reciting the *mātṛkā-mantra*, uttering the mantra for each [syllable]. With the words "I consecrate" (*abhiṣiñcāmi*), one should perform the consecration upon the head. Likewise, the procedure for the worship of the *tattvas* and the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) is the same.

There, the preceptor should accomplish the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) in the directions beginning with Indra. [He should perform] the *aruṇāsana-mudrā* and the *bhūta-mantras* with [offerings of] mango shoots, according to the day and the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
Regarding the six rites (*ṣaṭkarma*) during travel, each is performed separately; therein, first, for the accomplishment of all rites, the sun is the means for determining the East.

At sunrise, when Kṛttikā is in the east, or between Citrā and Svātī at dawn, one should purify the ground there with effort, such as by digging. One should discard husks, charcoal, stones, hair, and ashes. The practitioner (*mantrī*) should establish a beautiful, level line. In its center, he should plant a sharp-pointed stake (*śaṅku*), and there the shadow is observed.

One should plant a straight, firm *śaṅku* (gnomon) with a thick base, made of wood such as *khadira*, twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length. Using a cord measured by half the diameter [of the gnomon], one should describe a circle; then, one should place the *śaṅku* in its center. On the designated day, having observed the shadow at the eastern and western points [of the circle] according to this very measurement, one should diligently divide the space according to the supreme method. Then, the wise man should mark two points and drop a cord between them; that is declared in the *Nigama* to be known as the East (*prācī*). Crossing both ends of that cord, one should rotate...

In this manner, one should draw two fish in the south-western and north-eastern intermediate directions (vidiś) using the measurement of an even thread to form a square mandala. Then, in another way, one should accomplish the intermediate directions in succession. Thereafter, one should make it double the size of the middle thread; below that, one should make a mark (lāñchana), and with half of that [measurement], another mark. Having fixed the middle thread, one should then pull the string; wherever the mark of that [fish] falls, one should place a sign there. In this very same manner, the others in the intermediate directions [should be drawn].

In that manner, one should cause the recitation of mantras (*japa*), fire oblations (*homa*), and other rites to be performed with wealth. One should have a square enclosure (*kuṇḍa*) constructed measuring one cubit; its dimension is recorded as being exactly one cubit, which is known to be twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

This measurement is based on the middle joint of the middle finger of either the practitioner’s right hand or that of the preceptor (*ācārya*). The square enclosure, measuring one cubit, should be very beautiful, endowed with all the proper characteristics, and marked by four fish-designs (*matsya*). Having divided the square field into five parts by drawing lines, two and a half [parts] are for the *yama* (the boundary line).

One should extend this [line] by six finger-breadths; then, according to the measurement of the tip, one should divide the middle into four parts. With a measurement equal to half of half the corner, the wise one should draw a circle at half that distance. Starting from those two "fish" (formed by the intersections), one should mark the front. The womb of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍayoni*) should be as beautiful as an *aśvattha* leaf. Having prepared the field as before and divided it again into ten parts, the knower of the system should discard one space each in the middle and above. By that same measurement, one should cast a cord at the front; thus the fire-pit, resembling a half-moon, is delightful and bestows all accomplishments. [The square is] the four-cornered one.

One should place the prepared field on its two sides with a measurement of six *aṅgulas*, and then one should lay down three lines from the front above; thus the excellent *kuṇḍa* is established. According to the measure of the middle line, excluding another eighteenth part, one should place each [line] individually and then rotate [the cord] at half of that. This is declared to be the circular *kuṇḍa*, beautiful and captivating. A wise person should divide the square field into eight parts; one should place each part on both sides of the middle line. In this very same manner, one should place the lines above and below according to the measurement.

Then one should provide a hexagon; that is the excellent six-cornered fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having divided the square into eighteen parts by means of a thread, one should place one part outside at the end of the thread, both below and above.

By that measurement of the thread-parts, one should cause nine circles to be made. One should arrange three circles there for the pericarp and so forth. This is declared to be the lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*), which is dear to Padma (Lakṣmī) and captivating. The field made square is divided into twenty-four parts. Having set aside one part, one should again make it square. The inner square [is formed] from half the corner...

One should mark it according to the established measurements; from there, one should draw eight fish-figures from two corners. This sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is indicated as being one-sixth [of the total area] in all these cases. It is declared that the width of the pit should be equal to its length. The shape of the girdle (mekhalā) should correspond to the shape of the pit. One should place a single neck (kaṇṭha) outside with a depth of fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas). The measurement for the girdles is fifteen finger-breadths [for the first], and nine finger-breadths [for the others]. In a pit measuring one cubit (hasta), the girdles are two, four, and four finger-breadths [respectively]. In a pit measuring two cubits, they are six, four, and six finger-breadths.

In a pit measuring eight cubits, the height of the girdles (mekhalās) shall be ten finger-breadths for each of the directions starting from the northeast; in a pit measuring ten cubits, they shall be eleven finger-breadths for each. All these girdles should have a thickness of two cubits, which is traditionally recorded as thirty-three finger-breadths. A measurement of four cubits is recorded as fifteen finger-breadths per cubit, while a measurement of eight cubits is recorded as seventy-eight finger-breadths per cubit.
The length of the yoni at half the width of the pit is recorded as eight finger-breadths; one should place it facing downwards, equal in size to the face of an elephant.
