Having established [the base] above the girdle (*mekhalā*), one should place a stalk (*nāla*) shaped like a stalk, measuring slightly less than one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in height, in the middle. There, starting from the spot where the thread was removed, one should lead the thread into the opening of the womb (*yonirandhra*). Having joined it at the sides above the glans (*meḍhra*), and having cast it into the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should contemplate the tip of the womb as having an opening of one finger-breadth and a face of four finger-breadths, in the shape of a lotus. One should fashion nine parts there and arrange the pericarp (*karṇikā*) upon them; the filaments (*kesara*) and the petals of the pericarp should be made with three parts each, according to the sequence.

Having established me in the center of the *kuṇḍa*, the height should be four finger-breadths; likewise, one should avoid the *yoni* in a *yoni-kuṇḍa* and the lotus in a lotus-shaped *kuṇḍa*. [Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. I shall now describe the procedure for recitation (*japa*) for the sake of attaining success (*siddhi*), as it has been taught in its proper scope: the practitioner should accomplish the ritual applications (*prayoga*) there, such as the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) and others. By resorting to the proper location for the lamp, the practice of recitation, fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth becomes fruitful; otherwise, it will be fruitless. One should divide the square field into nine parts.

The wise man should write the pairs of vowels starting from the front (east) in the middle square and so forth in sequence. Having written the eight groups of consonants (*varga*), he should write them in the order starting from the front. Then, in due order, he should designate the mouth, the two hands, the sides, the two feet, and finally the tail. Wherever the lamp is placed within that field—be it a country, a tortoise-shaped site, a mountain, a city, a village, a temple of Śiva, or a palace—one should determine its location from the lowest to the highest. [If the lamp is] in the mouth, one gains [prosperity]; if in the hand, one becomes short-lived; if in the chest, one becomes indifferent; and if standing on the foot, there is suffering.

The wise one should divide the square field into nine parts. Having drawn it in the shape of a lotus, this seat bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). With the mantra *viyat* (the letter *ha*) joined with *bhṛgu* (the letter *sa*), and from the crescent moon (*indu-khaṇḍa*), one should write [the seed-syllable] in the central square. One should inscribe the vowels starting from the east, and having inscribed the eight groups of consonants (*varga-aṣṭaka*), one should inscribe the plough-shaped mark (*lāṅgala-āga*). This is declared to be the *Mṛtyuñjaya* seat, which bestows all accomplishments. I shall now describe the means for accomplishing the six rites (*ṣat-karma*); one should worship the six female messengers (*ṣaḍ-dūtī*). One should worship Rati, who is red; Vada, who is white; the beautiful Vāṇī; Aruṇā; Mahālakṣmī; Jyeṣṭhā, who has the luster of a lotus; and Nīlaśyāmā.

One should worship Māṃ, Mahādurgā, Prabhā, Kṛṣṇā, and Kālikā—endowed with these characteristics—at the beginning of the rite and so forth. Īśāna, Uttara, Pūrva, Nihṛti, Māruta, and Āgneyī are declared as the six [directions] prescribed for the six rites and others. The measure of a day and night is said to be sixty ghaṭikās; having divided that into six parts, one should calculate ten ghaṭikās each.

Starting from sunrise, one should proceed in the proper sequence: in spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, and also in hemanta and śiśira, one should accomplish one's respective rite, whether it be pacification (śānti) or...

In the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should remain in a secluded place; for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), the cool season (*śiśira*) is prescribed; for the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), the summer (*grīṣma*); and for the great rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the rainy season (*varṣā*) is said to be the rule. For the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), autumn (*śarad*) is prescribed; having understood this, one should accomplish the task. The lotus posture (*kamalāsana*) should be known as that which brings about all peace; the *svastika* posture is said to be the supreme means for all acts of subjugation. The *vikaṭa* posture is prescribed for immobilization; for causing enmity, the cock posture (*kukkuṭāsana*); for eradication, the thunderbolt posture (*vajrāsana*); and for killing, the elephant posture (*bhadra*) is proclaimed. For each specific rite, there are distinct mudrās; one should employ those respective mudrās.

One should display the mudrās of the lotus, the noose, the mace, the pestle, and the sword; they say the eighth is the vajra. One should employ [these] for pacification and other rites. The mantra consisting of the five elements should be applied to the six activities: it is said that water is used for pacification (śāntika); fire is impelled for subjugation (vaśya); earth is declared for paralyzing (stambhana); space for the rite of hatred (vidveṣa); wind for expulsion (uccāṭana); and fire for killing (māraṇa). Having correctly understood the rising of the elements and being joined with their respective maṇḍalas, the practitioner, desiring the welfare [of others], should employ them in those various rites. One should first join the cool-rayed moon (the lunar element) for one hundred thousand [recitations].

One should apply that respective seed-syllable [to] the wind of the earth (kṣoṇīcamāruta). Then, Śrīkaṇṭha, Bhārabhūtiśa, and Nakulīśa; likewise, the end of the first group (ka-varga) and the second group (ca-varga), one should extract the third [letter]. One should write the fourth and the fifth, measured by the letters of the groups; this is called the "letter of space" (ākāśalipi). Another letter is the "wind" (māruta); it consists of three dots (trivindu), Bhautikeśa, and ends with Mahākāla. One should extract the first letters of the five groups and Śānti as well; this is called another "letter of wind."

One should extract the fire (ra), the thirteenth [letter] from the two threads (the letter *sa*), and the nectar (the letter *ha*). One should also extract the second of the five groups (the letter *pa*) and the Lord of Bhṛgu (the letter *sa*). This is declared to be the fire-syllable (*lipivahni*). Next, one should write the water-syllable (*jalākṣara*), which consists of equal letters; having written it, one should oneself write the fourteenth [letter]. One should apply in sequence the fourth from the first [group] (the letter *ja*), the fourth from the second [group] (the letter *tha*), the end of *ḍa* (the letter *ṇa*), the end of *pa* (the letter *ma*), and likewise the end of *ca* (the letter *ṅa*). This is known as the water-syllable (*jalavarṇa*). One should extract the earth-syllable (*bhūmivarṇa*); having written the earth-syllable of Hari (the letter *la*), the mantra is thus: *ha sa pa sa ja tha ṇa ma ṅa la*. Then the five-fold number and the mantra... twice.

One should extract the third letter three times, and again the third letter three times, followed by the lords of Pisces and Capricorn in due order; this is declared to be the supreme *bhūtalipi*, which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). First is *grathana* (stringing), second is *vidarbhaṇa* (interlacing), third is *saṃpuṭa* (enclosing), and fourth is *rodhana* (obstructing). Fifth is said to be *yogi* (union), and the sixth is remembered as *pallava* (sprout). One should likewise write the letters of the mantra and the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in between. One should know that *grathana* is highly recommended for rites of pacification (*śāntika*). Having written the letters of the mantra's name, [one writes] the letters of the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

One should write "Raṃ"—this is declared to be the *vidarbhaṇa* (interlacing), the supreme method for bringing others under one's control (*vaśya*). One should utter the mantra at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end of the name; this is called *saṃpuṭa* (enclosing), and it is prescribed for the purpose of immobilizing (*stambhana*). When the name is placed at the beginning and the mantra is repeated in the middle, and the name is uttered again at the end, this is known as *rodhana* (obstructing), which is recommended for the sphere of causing enmity (*vidveṣa*). Placing the name of the target (*sādhya*) at the end of the mantra is likewise used for the practice of expulsion (*uccāṭana*). They know that placing the mantra at the end of the name is for the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*). Furthermore, [the mantras] are described as being white, reddish, yellow, variegated, black, and smoke-colored. Thus is the mantra [described].

The Ṛṇopidevatās attain the fruit in this very manner and not otherwise. For the sake of protecting one's own body, one should always perform the Mṛtyuñjaya [rite]; however, the ritual application (*prayoga*) should not be performed if one desires the full fruit, for from such application there is only minor accomplishment—thus spoke Śaṅkara. [Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. Now I shall proclaim the Nyāsa, the essence that grants all accomplishments (*siddhi*), by the mere knowledge of which the realization of the body arises. It was practiced in the Kṛta, Tretā, and even in the Dvāpara age; all the deities were manifest to their devotees.

The goddess Dhīnāhi was revealed by the compassionate ocean-like Guru Vīra through the pure awakening of the secret convention (*saṃketa*). In the Kali age, one should cultivate devotion to Śiva through the union of Kula and Akula, wherein the goddess Kālikā is directly perceived within the Kula. One should cause the Great Kāla to break open within the Kula during the union of Mahākāla and Kālikā. If the root power is always afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the pain of desire, the practitioner does not recognize her, and the perfection of mantra does not arise. At the root, the entire universe—both stationary and moving—is composed of phonemes.

The three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are the forms of knowledge and action arising from Māyā; Kālikā herself is the transformation in the form of Prakṛti. She is the form of the letters and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), bestowing success through *japa*, *homa*, and other rites. Through the distinction between yoga and enjoyment (*bhoga*), she is the means for the five *mudrās* and other practices; Kālī is the bestower of yoga, enjoyment, and all perfections (*siddhis*). I shall now declare the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) as it was spoken by Rudra: the letter mounted on the wheel of fire (R), joined with the three qualities (U) and the bindu (M); likewise, the pair of letters (KṢA), then the seven *māyā*-seeds (HŪṂ), then Mīneśa (I), and likewise Raurava (RA).

One should draw the third [wheel] on a surface made of *bhāra* wood, endowed with the *draṃ*, *sūkṣma*, and *śaṃca*. Therein, one should write Cakrī, Nārāyaṇa, Śravaṇī, Mādhava, Caṇḍī, Ekādaśī, and Mīna—this sevenfold seed-syllable ending with *dviṭha* (*svāhā*), O Goddess, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. Here, there is no consideration of *siddha*, *ari*, or *sādhya*; nor is there a wheel for gain or loss. There is no purification required for month, lunar day, fortnight, day, weekday, or asterism; nor is there any restriction of time, nor of what is fit or unfit to eat, through such effort. By the sequence of the Great Veneration (*mahārcana*) alone, the ritual action becomes the cause for success in yoga.

One should perform the ritual of the *samaya* at night using the *vati* (wick) and other materials; through the union of the left and right [channels], she bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). I shall now describe the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-samaya*) as it is taught in the *Rudrajāmala*: one should purify the ground there, as well as the charcoal and other elements. Having made it resemble the surface of a mirror or pure crystal, one should apply an ointment of *alinā* and *yakṣakardama*. There, one should arrange a beautiful triangle with level lines. Having drawn a dot (*bindu*) in its center, one should draw a lotus with eight petals (*brahma-padmada*) upon it. In the middle of that, one should place the *Śakti* described in the *Kula* tradition, who is soft and playful.

Having bathed according to the prescribed rite, the preceptor should enter the sacrificial mandala. He should perform all the preliminary rites, such as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), in the same manner as for Tāriṇī. Therein, he should establish the three principles (*tatvatraya*) and the realization of the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasādhana*). These are: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara; following that, Śuddhavidyā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati;
and further, Vidya, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Ahaṃkāra, and then again: skin, eyes, tongue, nose, mind, intellect, speech, hands, and feet.

The anus and genitals are impelled [by the elements]; likewise sound, touch, form, taste, smell, space, wind, fire, water, earth, and again the wind as the soul of all—first, the seed-syllable born of speech (*vāgbhava*), joined with the sixteenth vowel (the nasal *anusvāra*). Again, the four beginning with earth are said to be one with the vowel. Or rather, having uttered the speech-born seed-syllable, one should recite "This Viṣṇu strode forth," and "To the self, to the principle of the self. One should then utter the word "I purify the gross body" (*svāhā*) for the purification of the principle. Then, having uttered the "king of desire" (*kāmarāja*):

One should perform purification with the mantra "Sūkṣma" for the twenty principles beginning with Śiva—namely the five groups starting with *ka* (the *kādi* group), ending with *ra*, along with *sa* and *va*—and for the principle of *Vidyā*. Then, having uttered the third [seed-syllable] and again the fifteenth letter, one should extract the principle beginning with the foot (*pāda*) which consists of all that is to the left (*vāma*). One should utter the word "Śivatattva," which is the purification of the body and the individual soul (*jīva*). Having uttered the third [syllable], one should worship *Prakṣa* the fourth time, and then, having uttered [the mantra]...

Having repeatedly recited all the *tattvas* and the purification of the other body, one should utter the supreme mantra ending in *svāhā*. Therein, one should purify the *śakti* and thereafter perform the purification. One should perform the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) for both [the practitioner and the *śakti*] just as in the case of *Tāriṇī*. Through purification, one should purify the *śakti*; having purified the excellent woman who is the pure *śakti*, one should then perform the purification of the divine face and the excellent limbs. One should mutter the great mantra of Mahākāla one hundred and eight times, as well as the *praṇava*.

One should extract the seed-syllable (bīja) of Hṛllekhā-Kaulinī, but then one should utter the seed-syllable of Kartṛkā and [the name] Mahākāla. Having uttered the Prāsāda seed-syllable, [one says] "to Mahādeva" followed by that. [One utters] Krodhīśa mounted on Fire (Ra), with the left eye (I) and the bindu (M). After the word "to Kālikā," one should extract the Prāsāda seed-syllable. Mahākāla is Mahādeva, the bestower of all siddhis. May the Goddess Bhagavatī Caṇḍī, Caṇḍikā, of fierce prowess, the southern [power], be pleased.

One should extract the mantra *lī svāhā*. Then, one should perform meditation upon the Supreme Goddess in the heart-cakra (*hṛccakra*): Cāmuṇḍā, the divine southern [form], with a terrifying face, fierce, with disheveled hair, and four arms;

adorned with a garland of severed heads, holding in her upper left lotus-hand a sword with a head recently severed, and in her upper right hand granting fearlessness and boons; having the luster of a great cloud, dark-complexioned, clad in the directions as raiment, and adorned with skulls.

[She is] smeared with blood dripping from rows of skulls fixed upon her head, terrifying with a pair of corpses as ear-ornaments, possessing formidable fangs and a gaping mouth, with breasts that are full and high, having made a girdle from a multitude of hands of the dead, laughing with a face whose mouth is widened by streams of blood flowing from both corners. Of terrible form and most fierce, she dwells in the cremation ground.

There stands the great and fierce Mahākāla, naked and clad in the directions (the sky), holding a skull and a sickle in his left [hands], and a trident and a staff in his right; his limbs are adorned with serpents, and he is further decorated with garlands of ashes and bones, standing in the midst of a blazing fire.

Established upon a bed in a cremation ground, with the woman positioned in the reverse posture, they should consume drinks, foods, and chewables while gazing at one another. Meditating thus, one should worship the Goddess; then all perfections (*siddhi*) arise. One should perform correct meditation and worship within the *kula*-yantra—either on a plate of gold, silver, or the like, or upon a mandala drawn on the ground. Within a triangle, there is a lotus, and again another triangle within it;

thereafter, a nine-cornered figure (*navakoṇa*). In the center of that, one should place Śivā. Having inscribed the primordial Śakti, one should again inscribe the Śakti. Then, having inscribed the wheel of fire (*vahnicakra*)—

One should pierce the *hyaśakti* by means of the sequence for piercing the knots; one should expand the fire downward by the very sequence for piercing the knots, and likewise pierce the upper part of the *śakti*. By the expansion of the fire upward, one should pierce the fire within the channel (*vāha*). It is said that there are three [knots] of the *śakti* and two of the fire, ending toward the south. According to the ritual procedure for the worship of the seat (*pīṭha*), the wise one should worship the seat. Having worshipped the foundations (*ādhāra*) and so forth, he should worship the nine *śaktis*. Having invoked the *Sāraṅgī* there, he should worship her with ritual offerings (*upacāra*). Having raised the *Kuṇḍalinī*, he should pierce the *Brahma-granthi*; having brought her into the path of sound (*nāda*), he should establish her there.

Then, having pierced the *brahmagranthi* at the twelve-petaled lotus, one should satisfy [the deity] with that stream [of breath]. Having worshipped the Goddess in the heart, one should perform the external worship. Leading [the consciousness] through the central path of the *suṣumnā* into the interior of the *viṣṇu*, one should remain in meditation, contemplating the state consisting of *sāmarasya* (union), and perform the recitation (*japa*). Having invoked the Goddess residing there, one should pierce the *ājñā-cakra*. One should place her upon the nose via the central path of the nostrils. Having uttered the root mantra and awakened the word "Kālikā," [one should say]: "Come, come, O Great Goddess; establish yourself here with your two sandals. [One should then perform] the *saṃkalpa*, the *ātman*, and so forth, ending with the *yonimudrā*.

One should present the sixteen services (upacāras) beginning with water for the feet (pādya) and ending with the honey-mixture (madhuparka). Having worshipped Dakṣiṇākālī along with her attendants and her retinue, one should worship Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, and Vipracittā within the six corners of the fire-diagram (vahni-ṣaṭkoṇaka). Furthermore, one should worship Ugrā, Ugra, Prabhā, and Dīptā in the [other] triangles. Again, one should worship Nīlā, Dhanā, Balā, and Kā in the triangles. Likewise, in the lower triangle, one should worship Mātṛ, Mudrā, and Sitā. All of them are dark blue (śyāmā), holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) in their hands, adorned with garlands of severed heads (muṇḍamālā), and holding the heel of their left hand with the index finger.

Then, O Smṛtā, the Mothers are to be worshipped: Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, Aparājitā, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and likewise Nārasiṃhī. For all these goddesses, the offering of oblations (bali) and worship should be performed in due order with incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and so forth; thereafter, one should present the bali to the spirits (bhūta). Afterwards, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the rules through the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) beginning with the fire. Śrīnātha...

Having turned his face toward the disciple, the teacher faces him; in this manner, according to the sequence of Vedic initiation (*vedadīkṣā*), the piercing of the mantra (*mantravedha*) is performed gradually. Afterwards, he should give the nectar of the left (*vāmāmṛta*) and perform the purification of all the principles (*tattvas*). However, the Guru should utter the mantra into the right ear of the disciple. The Guru should then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), and so forth, upon the body of the disciple. The seer is indeed Bhairava, the deity is Uṣṇih, the meter is declared [to be that], the goddess is Dakṣiṇakālī, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *Lajjā* (Hrīṃ), and the pillar (*kīlaka*) is [the same].

The seed-syllable is *kūrca* (hrūṃ), while the power (*śakti*) and the application (*viniyoga*) are according to one's desire. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs, one should place the supreme syllable beginning with *ḍa* on the right calf; one should place the syllables beginning with *na* and ending with *kṣa* on the left calf. One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra, and one becomes identical with the Goddess herself. Furthermore, the true Guru should utter the mantra into the right ear either eight or twelve times, and having bestowed the mantra, he should offer it [to the disciple].

Furthermore, one who seeks dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa should first present before the Guru gold, a cow, an elephant, a horse, wealth, grain, and likewise cattle. Thereafter, he should satisfy the Guru’s capacity according to his means. He should feed the Brāhmaṇas there, as well as the women living in the lineage and young maidens. He should give abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and having offered salutations, ask for forgiveness. [Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi. I shall now describe the method of spiritual practice (sādhana). Śaṃ...

Listen to this most wonderful [teaching], by which through mere consciousness the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) is produced. First, one should purify the ground on a mountain, at a lake, on a riverbank, at a solitary *liṅga*, in a cremation ground, at a triple-pathway, or at a crossroads; or even in a temple of the Mothers (*mātṛgṛha*), in a thicket (*ujjaṭa*), or on a riverbank. Even though the practitioner has performed the preliminary consecration (*saṃskāra*), he should perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*). Purified by a fine, clean cloth, the wise man, eating only at night and subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), avoiding women and meat, should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.

Free from the two [periods of impurity], one should diligently perform the *homa* with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) or sesame seeds. Having bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure through daily rites and the like during the day, one should perform worship at night according to the description of the five mudrās. In this very manner, a wise person should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; being pure, one should perform the recitation during the day while attending to one's respective duties. One should likewise perform that same number of recitations at night through the application of the left and right [paths]. At night, the mouth should be filled with betel.

Established upon his bed, he should perform one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa-japa*), and he shall become a lord of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). He should employ gestures (*hāva*) and expressions (*bhāva*) and so forth; he will then become a great hero (*mahāvīra*). With that very [practice], he should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and always provide offerings of food, drink, and the like. Or else, I shall describe the practice (*sādhana*) in another manner: having thoroughly purified the place of recitation through efforts such as digging and so on, and having placed within it a great conch-shell and the five skulls (*pañcamuṇḍaka*).

In the midst [of this], one should perform the anointing and other rites for a great *preta* who is beautifully adorned with a *khaṇḍaṅga* (skull-ornament), and bathe him according to the prescribed rules. Having clothed him in red garments and applied collyrium to his eyes, one should place betel and other offerings in his mouth and apply red sandalwood paste to his forehead. One should then draw the worship-yantrogram—a triangle within a lotus—on the forehead; furthermore, one should draw this worship-yantrogram on the head, as well as on the hands and feet, using a sharp instrument.

Likewise, the wise man should fix wooden stakes made of *khadira* and other woods into the ground; he should tie a rope there with a firm knot. He should offer oblations (*bali*) upon each of the six petals and upon each stake individually. He should perform the ritual dismissal (*utsarga*) with milk, using black gram, meat, fish, three kinds of liquor, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and cakes. Having uttered the seed-syllable of action (*karmabīja*)—the letter *KṢ* mounted on fire (*R*), with the left eye (*I*) and the bindu (*M*)—and having uttered "to Śmaśānakālī," and having uttered the supreme mantra beginning with the first seed-syllable and ending with the weapon (*astra*) mantra, and having uttered the *māyābīja* (*Hrīṃ*), [he should worship] Mahākāla for Śmaśāna-Bhairava.

"O Lāyadeva, remover of all obstacles, O Hara! Accept the offering (*bali*) and dispel the obstacle; accept the offering and ward off the obstacle. This mantra, ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), is declared for the offering to Bhairava. Having uttered the seed-syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ), one should write that [syllable] along with its presiding deity. Then, one should place it upon the letter *agni* (ra), followed by the thirteenth vowel (*au*) with the bindu (*m*). The Rudras who dwell in the cremation ground are fond of offerings of bone and flesh. They shall properly ward off the obstacle while accepting the offering. [The mantra continues: "Ward off the obstacle, ward off the obstacle," and grant the boon. This mantra, ending with *dviṭha*, is declared for the offering to Rudra.

Then one should write the triad *māyā-lajjā-tathālakṣmī* (the Illusion, the Modesty, and likewise the Fortune mantras), as well as *nārāyaṇa* and *sūkṣma*. Then *paraṃ tu madhusūdanaḥ*, followed by the word *yoginībhyaḥ*, and then *śmaśānavāsinī*. Then *pracaṇḍā caṇḍarūpā tatkartṛ-karparadhāriṇī*, the pair *baliṃ gṛhṇāpaya*, and the words *sarva-vighna-nivāraya varaṃ dehi*. One should utter the end with *viṭhāntaḥ*; this is the *yoginī-bali*. [The mantra for] *Kṣetrapāla* is *raudraṃ vahni-samārūḍhaṃ caturdaśa-svarānvitaṃ bindu-nāda-kalā-krāntaṃ kṣetrapālaṃ tuṅetakaṃ śmaśānavāsi*.

One should offer the *kṣetrapāla* bali after reciting the mantra ending with the syllable *viṭh*. Then, having recited the seed-syllable of Vārāhī, followed again by the seed-syllable ending in the fifth letter (Na), one should utter the words "to Vakratuṇḍa" and then the armor-mantra (*varma*). One should say the words "accept the bali" and "ward off obstacles. Furthermore, one should say "grant me success (*siddhi*). This is the supreme mantra ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). One whose body is the bliss of wine (*madirānanda*) should perform the placement of the vessel (*pātra*). Upon the Heart [mantra], one should place the Great Hero (*mahāvīra*), and upon Śiva, the Power (*śakti*). She is naked, with disheveled hair, holding a sword and a skull-bowl, and she covers...

One should worship the family yantra with the family substances, offering incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and the bali-offering of the five elements. One should perform the recitation (japa) of the root mantra along with its worship according to one's capacity. By performing sexual union with a woman who has reversed her [normal] state while standing upon a corpse, and by reciting there ten thousand times, one becomes a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis). When he is terrified by fear, they will devour him; therefore, when they say "Give! Give!", one should offer a goat as a bali. Violence must never be committed without the giving of a bali. The accomplishment of a mantra is certainly dependent upon the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). After that, I shall explain the fire sacrifice (homa).

One should diligently perform the *homa* in a triangular sacrificial pit (*yonikuṇḍa*) or even in a funeral fire. Having extracted a pair of creepers, one should likewise bring them into an unbaked earthen vessel; one should offer into the fire pure leaves of *nāgabalī* smeared with the creeper.

One should perform the *homa* with effort ten thousand times, or a thousand, or one hundred and eight times; by this, one shall bring the three worlds under control. The Goddess who rides upon a corpse (*sāraṅgīśavavāhinī*) becomes manifest before him, and he attains therein a perfection difficult to find in the three worlds. The practitioner becomes a master of speech, his wealth becomes like that of Vaiśravaṇa, he becomes a yogi equal to Dattātreya, and in enjoyment, he is like Indra.

O son of Pāṇḍu, he is indeed the wrath of Vaivasvata; O descendant of Bhṛgu, he is equal to Hariścandra in renunciation and like the son of Bhr̥gu in mantras. He is supreme in prowess, the mother of Janī, [active] in strength, and dear to Varuṇī.

By the mere knowledge of him, the eight siddhis will certainly be attained. Having divided the mantra into three parts, one should diligently perform the homa; one should offer oblations of meat, sesame, red hair, curd, rice, and milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with the three sweets.

One should bring the three worlds under one's control; furthermore, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) using visible honey and sugarcane juice, as well as streams of blood and marrow—the wise man should satisfy [the deity] with these very substances. At the conclusion of the libation, the great mantra-practitioner should perform the auspicious worship of the Virgin Goddess (*Kumārī*), including the rites of invocation and so forth, and worship her with the *madhuparka* offering. One should worship the lineage of the Virgin Goddess with ritual services (*upacāra*). One should satisfy Mahākālī with that [offering], pouring a stream of blood over the *kula*.
He who diligently offers the blood of a rat, a cat, a human, a ram, and a buffalo goes to the world of the Goddess. Poetic talent arises in him, and he becomes like another Bṛhaspati. Like a god...

Having become new, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation; such a man becomes liberated while living, free from the effects of sinful or meritorious karma. One should offer the first oblation to the god Mahākāla consisting of ghee, meat, fat, blood, sugar, black flowers, and honey—especially with blood. Having beheld the blossoming temple of the Kula, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. By reciting it with the realization of non-difference, regarding the Guru as [the deity] himself, one attains union (sāyujya). For one who is unable [to perform this], he should recite it four hundred thousand times, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), during the day, with hair unbound, and naked, facing the cardinal directions. Through the homa of red flowers, there is the attainment of mantra-perfection.

A wise man, seeing a naked woman as his single focal point, should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; his speech shall become priceless poetry consisting of both prose and verse. Likewise, having worshipped according to the rules a beautiful and excellent woman in a cremation ground, a forest, a mountain, or at a crossroads, the practitioner should touch her vulva and her lingam while reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times as his focal point; having done so, he shall attain great wisdom and become a leader among poets.

Alternatively, in a secluded place or according to the tradition of his own family, a man should recite the mantra ten thousand times while focusing on his own tongue as the "world of the vulva"; like a supreme practitioner of mantras, he shall master the Vedas and Shastras that were previously unheard.

The practitioner of mantra should recite ten thousand times (*ayuta*) while touching the *bhaga*; this is prescribed as the expiation for both major and minor sins. A man should perform anointing with creepers (*latābhyaṅga*) and likewise recite ten thousand times; then kings will come under his control, as will the women of the city. During the anointing with creepers, the practitioner of mantra should recite for the sake of liberation from great sins. Or, in the absence of creepers, the practitioner of mantra should carefully remove [the hair], take it in his own hand, and having recited [the mantra], he becomes a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

The practitioner, having risen in the morning, should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with a concentrated mind. The wise one, having joined the limbs [of the deity] with his own limbs upon the body of Śakti, should perform the *nyāsa*. He should recite everything—recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and libation (*tarpaṇa*)—as being identical with Her. One must not show them contempt, nor strike them even with a flower. Crookedness, unpleasant speech, and the withholding of food, drink, and so forth, as well as binding, must never be done; for success arises from women, and they are the creation and the sustenance of women. The maintenance of the world... [text ends].

She who acts as the destroyer of all things is indeed the Goddess; otherwise, no supernatural power (*siddhi*) arises. By means of the Mahācīna-krama alone, the practitioner (*mantrī*) should diligently recite the mantra over the *latāpuṣpa* (creeper-flower) and the water of the creeper; she herself shall become a wish-fulfilling vine (*kalpalatā*).

Having worshipped the three leaves of the *mahācīnakramalatā* and the *lañjā* plants in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), the best of practitioners (*sādhakottama*) should recite it a thousand times; then he attains sovereignty and is never overcome by fear. With his own blood...

Garlands made of coral or silver, strung with knots of *ākuśa* grass, bestow all fruits of happiness, O Dear One; a garland strung with fibers (*nāḍī*) grants great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*). A garland of thirty beads yields the fruit of sovereignty; one of twenty-five grants liberation; one of fourteen bestows the liberation of *mayī*; and the Goddess consisting of fifteen beads is established for the rites of killing (*māraṇa*), driving away (*uccāṭana*), paralyzing (*staṃbhana*), deluding (*mohana*), subjugating (*vaśya*), obstructing (*nirodha*), and the magic ointment (*añjana*). For the attainment of the power of the sandals (*pādukāsiddhi*), the number of beads is proclaimed to be one hundred. Alternatively, one should make it one hundred and eight, which grants all desires. One should always perform the recitation (*japa*) with the hands, but not for optional rites (*kāmya*) due to a lack of understanding; even for optional rites, one may perform it with the hands.

O Priyaṃvadā, one should perform the finger-counting (aṅgulijapa) here; one should recite with the fingers including the thumb. Any rite performed without the thumb becomes fruitless. The finger-garland (karamālā) is proclaimed to extend from the two joints of the ring finger, in order starting from the little finger, up to the base of the index finger. Circumambulating the Meru (the middle phalanx of the thumb) starting from the base joint of the ring finger—reciting otherwise, due to the fault of leaping over the Meru, yields no fruit. Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction, one should recite across the eight joints up to the base of the middle finger; the tip of the middle finger is [the end].
Taking the middle joint of the ring finger as Mount Meru, one should not cross over it; the practitioner should join the tips of the index fingers there. For him, four things will surely perish:

life, knowledge, fame, and strength. One should not separate the fingers; one should slightly contract the palm. Now, therefore, I shall describe the stringing of the rosary which awakens the infinite reality.

Having performed worship with devotion, being pure and having fasted beforehand, the practitioner, having performed his daily rites, being pure, a knower of mantras, and observing the auspicious constellations, should himself string the rosary in a solitary place while maintaining silence at the appropriate time.
With great care, one should select grains that are of equal appearance, neither too large nor too small, free from insects and other defects, washed clean, and fresh.

These should be stirred separately with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Then, O best of the twice-born, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of three strands—without knots, tripled again, and either of silk (*paṭṭasūtra*), smooth, red, or black, depending on whether the rite is for peace (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśa*), or malevolent magic (*abhicārika*)—is placed upon nine horse-leather leaves in the shape of a lotus. The thread and the gems are then washed with scented water in a mechanical vessel.

One should cast [the beads] into cemetery water, or water from a well, a pedestal, or a bathing place; with pure water, blood, musk, and saffron. Having placed the *tāra*, the *śakti*, the *mātṛkā*, and [the seed-syllables] upon the thread and the gems, one should worship them with offerings and perform oblations according to one's capacity. If one is unable to perform the rite of homa, one should perform double the recitation (*japa*). Taking each gem one by one, the wise man should join it to the thread; joining mouth to mouth, he should fix tail to tail. It should be made like a cow’s tail, or it may have any shape at all. One should place a single knot of the same material at the front. One by one...

One should fashion the Brahma-knot at the center; having thus prepared the rosary for recitation, one should then perform the consecration ritual. One should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the Sadyojāta mantra and its waters. One should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and camphor using the Vāmadeva mantra. One should fumigate it with the Aghora and Tatpuruṣa mantras. One should consecrate each [bead] individually one hundred times with the fifth mantra, "Īśāna" (beginning with *praṇava*). The great mantra beginning with *praṇava* is always [to be used].

Following the sequence of the *śiviti*, one should consecrate the Meru-stūpa with that very fifth mantra. Having thus prepared the rosary (*akṣamālā*), the wise practitioner should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) therein. O Lord of Gods, having worshipped it with devotion using the root mantra, and having worshipped the Guru, one should receive the rosary from his hand. One who is impure must not touch it, nor should one show it even to the Guru. The wise man should perform the recitation (*japa*) on the middle finger when eating, after eating, or when joyful. For subsequent rites, one should recite using the thumb and ring finger. For the rites of killing (*māraṇa*) and driving away (*uccāṭana*), one should recite by joining the index finger with the thumb. For the rite of killing, one should recite by joining the little finger with the thumb. At the conclusion of the recitation—

Having worshipped that rosary, one should keep it concealed; at the time of recitation, that auspicious recitation rosary must be protected. O learned one, one should reveal the Guru, but never the mantra; one should never reveal either the rosary or the vidyā.

Since spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, rākṣasas, and cāraṇas seize [the power] when it is made manifest, therefore one should practice it in secret. If the thread becomes worn out, one should re-knot that thread and perform a hundred recitations. If, through negligence, it falls from the hand, one should recite one hundred and eight [times]. Even if it has been touched by those whose contact is forbidden, one should move it and perform the recitation as is appropriate. Thus, O Goddess, the rosary for recitation on this earth has been described by me.

"Difficult to obtain and always to be hidden even without effort, if you are my beloved. [Thus ends the second chapter of the Muṇḍamālā. "O God of gods, O beautiful one who is the essence of bliss, having worshipped ten thousand times with *bilva* leaves at a sacred site or a seat of practice during a great night in the cremation ground, one attains equality with Vāgīśa (the Lord of Speech). [Thus ends the eleventh chapter on optional and obligatory rites in the Cūḍāmaṇi. Now, the *Muṇḍamālā*: "I bow to the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, who consists of universal bliss, who is eternal, who is saluted by all the Āmnāyas, and who bestows all supernatural powers (*siddhis*). The Goddess said: "O God of gods, O Great God, O delighter of supreme bliss!"

"O one with a pleasing face, be gracious and speak, O lover of sweet words! Reveal that which is hidden from the five-faced Lord in all the Tantras and Mantras—known as the 'Secret' (Guhyākhya)—if I am indeed dear to you. Śiva said: "How shall I tell you the secret, O fickle-minded one? By your very nature as a woman, you do not know the Great Principle (Mahattattva) that bestows liberation. The Goddess said: "I shall become perfectly steady; this must never be spoken [of me], for when I have become a jewel..."

O Śi0u0va, the single-pointed contemplation (*ekabhāvana*) of the deity, the guru, and the mantra is declared [to be liberation]. The mantra is indeed the guru, and that guru is the deity. Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Vidyā, Dhūmāvatī, as well as Vagalā, Siddhividyā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalā—these ten Mahāvidyās have been proclaimed by Mahādeva.

They are extremely difficult to obtain in the worlds and are honored by the six Āmnāyas. These supreme Vidyās are rare in the three worlds; they grant happiness and liberation, are eternal, and cannot be accomplished through mere hardship or meditation.

I shall tell you everything, out of pure affection, by what means one attains accomplishment on this earth; here there is no requirement for perfected adepts (*siddhas*) and the like, nor any consideration of constellations and so forth, no purification of time and the like, and no defect regarding enemies and such. The *Siddhavidyā* and *Mahāvidyā* are easily accessible and free from exertion; O Great Goddess, there is never anything whatsoever that is difficult to accomplish. That which is the supreme *Vidyā*, Kālī, is proclaimed as Tārā; and that which is the supreme *Vidyā*, Tārā, was previously declared to be fourfold. Indeed, through the differentiation of these two, various mantras come into being. And it has been said in the *Kālikā*:

In this *Tārā-kalpa*, I have previously described the sixteenth Great Vidyā in four ways according to the distinctions of the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī and others; here, the fifth would be that which is devoid of the seed-syllable of the Ekākṣarī Mahāvidyā. The three-eyed Great Goddess Bhuvaneśī has been proclaimed [as such]. The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, these Vidyās have been seen and spoken by you, yet they have not been revealed. Now, out of a spirit of compassion, O beautiful one, tell me for our delight. Śiva said: "This Great Vidyā of Bhuvaneśī was formerly propitiated by the King of the Gods (Indra), who was deluded by the name Vajra. She is the Ekākṣarī, devoid of seed-syllables, radiant with the *vāgbhava* [syllable], and known as the source of the letter 'Ja'."

This Vidyā, born of the lineage of Siddhas, was formerly worshipped by Śakra, the wielder of the flower-bow; it was established in the world by Bhuvaneśī. This Vidyā, which is the Maiden (Kumārī), was truly transmitted by you, O Satyavatī. Established solely by me in the form of Śiva and solely in the form of Śakti, this Vidyā is Tārā, whose nature is like the moon. Bhairavī is the Great Vidyā who bestows great prosperity; Chinnamastā is fond of wine and meat, and her own nature is red. Dhūmāvatī is the Great Vidyā devoted to killing and driving away enemies. Vagalā is endowed with various qualities such as subjugation and paralyzing. Mātaṅgī is the Great Vidyā.

"The lotus that brings the three worlds under control is said to be threefold; likewise, it exists as the single-syllable [mantra]. When alone, it bestows great prosperity and grants both happiness and liberation. [Thus ends the first chapter of the Muṇḍamālā-tantra. The Goddess said: "The rosary has been described with effort, yet it has not been fully revealed. What is the name of this 'rosary of beads' (akṣamālā), and what is its fruit? Please tell me. The Lord said: "O Queen of the Gods, the rosary of beads (akṣamālā) is of many kinds according to the division of desired purposes. Listen..."

Now, in this highly praised [work], it is described by me at length through a garland of phonemes arranged in both direct and reverse order, following the sequence from *a* to *kṣa* and from *kṣa* to *a*, according to the method of the Supreme Goddess. One must never overstep the letter *kṣa*, which is the form of Mount Meru; for that garland which lacks *Meru* or which oversteps *Meru* is devoid of faith, utterly obscure, and fruitless. That supreme [garland] consists of one hundred and twenty threads, having entered the central channel (*brahmanāḍī*), and it should be known as strung together by that [channel], bestowing the fruits of all rites. At the beginning, after performing one hundred and eight recitations (*japa*), one should practice the "neuter" (*klība*). As for the two phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ*, they are declared to be the "excessive neuter. *Note on terminology:* * *Anuloma-viloma*: Direct (forward) and reverse (backward) order. * *Ādi-kṣānta-kṣādi-kānta*: From *a* to *kṣa*; from *kṣa* to *a*. * *Kṣakāra*: The syllable *kṣa*. * *Meru*: The central peak/letter representing the axis of the alphabet-garland. * *Aśraddhā*: Lacking faith/devotion. * *Citriṇī*: The variegated or central thread/channel. * *Brahmanāḍī*: The central channel of the subtle body. * *Klība*: Neuter vowels (*ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ*) used here in a specific ritual context. * *Iṣṭottara-śata*: One hundred and eight. * *Japa*: Recitation. * *Va*: This final *va* likely marks the end of the verse or section.

Furthermore, according to the sequence of desired distinctions, there are eight classes [of beads] beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śa*. A rosary made of crystal grants liberation; one made of lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*) grants many sons; one made of *jīvaputra* seeds grants wealth; and one made of stones grants all enjoyments. O Dear One, a rosary of impure crystal bestows great prosperity. A rosary made from the wood of the *dhattūra* plant found in cremation grounds, used in the rite of *Dhūmāvatī*, grants all accomplishments and bestows liberation, O Fair Lady. A rosary strung from the bones of human fingers, regardless of the specific variety, grants all perfections and bestows liberation. It should be strung using a cord or even a red cloth, and it must always be guarded with great effort.

O beloved, a rosary made of *mātṛkāja* seeds is said to grant fivefold results and bestow the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). A rosary strung with pearls bestows the fruit of all sovereignty. Furthermore, mantras using gems, jewels, and coral grant perfect success in every respect. Regarding the place: O Goddess, I have described to you the locations—on a riverbank, at the foot of a *vilva* tree, in a cremation ground, in a pure dwelling, at a great *liṅga*, on a mountain, or wherever the mind finds its dissolution. Now, tell me of the seat (*āsana*).

Now, for the sake of all accomplishments (*siddhi*), a tiger skin is prescribed; for the accomplishment of knowledge (*jñāna-siddhi*), a deer skin; a cloth seat removes disease; one made of cane increases affection; silk is said to bestow nourishment; and a woolen blanket (*kaṃbala*) grants all accomplishments. Whether it be white or black—especially a red woolen blanket—one should bring a soft blanket that has fallen on a battlefield, or even one killed by a beast, or the skin of a dead man. Or else, O Goddess, one should take the skin from the womb of women who have miscarried, or skin from those in the prime of youth; this bestows all accomplishments and grants the abundance of all enjoyments. One should prepare [the seat] with such skins.

The seat for the *ekavīra* (solitary hero) rite is a throne made from the wood of a cremation ground, or a seat fashioned from the timber of a formidable river-bank tree. One who has been initiated should enter [the ritual space] wearing a garment of animal skin. There, neither a slave nor a female slave, but rather a *snātaka* or a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), should prepare a square pit, four fingers deep on all sides, measuring one cubit or two cubits in extent. Upon that pure seat, one should perform the consecration and worship. The lotus posture (*padmāsana*) bestows enjoyment and grants yoga; the tortoise posture (*kaurmāsana*) is likewise mentioned. They say this lotus posture yields all fruits. This is the *ekavīrāsana*.

O Goddess, standing with feet upward, adorned with the *virodha* [mudrā], this best of all postures is indeed difficult even for the gods to perform; it grants all accomplishments (*siddhi*) to men. O Mistress of Gods, when one worships the Goddess at night while situated in the subterranean chamber (*pātālagṛha*) in the *padmāsana* posture, one becomes wealthy and possessed of a chariot. O Goddess, among all seats (*pīṭhas*), there are four supreme seats:
the great seat Jālandhara, the great Pūrṇācala, O Great Goddess, Uḍḍīyāna, and likewise the great Kāmarūpa. Jālandhara is to be known as the preeminent in the Kṛta age, and in the Tretā...

In the Kṛta age it was Pūrṇagiri, in the Tretā age Uḍḍiyāna, and in the Kali age it is Kāmarūpa; in this world, it bestows great fruit and, by its mere sight, grants great spiritual perfection (siddhi). Among the fifty sacred seats (pīṭhas), Kāmarūpa yields the greatest fruit; there, O Goddess, even a single recitation, worship, or offering becomes equal to a hundred thousand. O Goddess, what need is there to describe its virtues? Since it exists in the form of the Yoni, what need is there to describe its virtues? (Iṣṭasiddhimuktāvalī, Tṛtīya Paṭala).

The Goddess said: "Caṇḍikā has become pleased by the offering of the *bali* alone. O Śaṅkara, reveal clearly that which was previously told to us. Īśvara said: "O Queen of the Gods, I shall describe this secret method of worship with the *bali*. Ascend [to your seat], O Rā, and remain now perfectly steady. [Offer] curd, milk, jaggery, food, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with sugar; milk-rice, honey, meat, *keśara*, and *modaka*; rabbit, mutton, ginger with sugar, and plantain."

One should offer as an oblation (bali) fruit, *laḍḍukas*, roasted grain, flour-cakes, *prāṇa*, fish, *pāṭīna*, *śakula*, and likewise *vikaṭa* and *madgara* fish; buffalo meat, O beautiful lady, bird meat, *ḍimbha* meat produced from various sources, black goat meat, great meat, *godhikā*, and likewise *hariṇī*; fish meat with water, and *godhikā* meat; various side dishes, milks, condiments, and honey;

smeared with slightly scorched ghee, at night or even during the day, especially on an auspicious day in the dark fortnight. When a goat is offered, one becomes eloquent; when a fish [is offered], [one gains] power.

If the gift is of an elephant, it shall certainly be so; in the case of a buffalo, there will be success in wealth, and in the case of a deer, the fruit shall be enjoyment. If the gift is of a bird, there is great prosperity, and if [the gift is] the supreme accomplishment of one's desire. The deities in the forehead, hands, heart, and the center of the *śakti* are the presiding deities of one’s own body. When blood is offered from one's own body, O Rudra-bodied one, or when another [offering] is given, great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) arises through the offering of a *caṇḍāla* as a sacrificial victim. O Lord of Gods, by the offering of a horse, [great power arises].
